PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS:

"IN LONDON," said the returned tourist boast. fully. "I appeared at Court." "How much was the fine?" queried the cynical friend. MRS. BROWNE : "What will you give towards a new bicycle for me?" Browne: "The wind for the tyres." SHE: "I don't look at all like myself to-day." He: "It would be a good time to have your picture taken."

FREDDIE : "Ma, what's baby's name?" Ma: "Baby hasn't any name yet." "Then how did he know he belonged here?" A SURE THlNG—Bobby: "Mamma, what is a lost cause ?' " Mother: "Any cause that your dear papa advocates, love." RomANTIo.—" All the world's a stage." Cynic: "Yes, and most of us never get any further than mere scene-shifters."
WHAT 18 that word of five letters of which, when you take away two, only one remains 1— St-me.

JACK: "Well, did you propose last night?" Torn: "Must have done it. I know I meant to do it, and I know we're engaged; so whatever I said must have been all right." THOMSON "That beggar, Anderson, gave our boy, Johnny, a drum for his birthday, but I soon made it all right." Smith: "What did you do?" Thomson: "I gave him a pocket-knife." "CONSIDER the chickens, my son, study their ways and be wise. Whenever they take to drink- ing their bills go up, and by keeping their bills down they find enough to eat." "TELL your master that that mutton had a most delicate flavour." Yes, mum. Yer see, it would ave a delicate flavour, the sheep being so delicate that it was killed so as it shouldn't die."

"Is your picture in the Academy a success?" "That's what lam wondering. Somebody said it was worth the price of admission." CLARA : "Was he bashful?" Maude: "I should say so. I had to tell him at last that I would certainly scream if he attempted to kiss me."

BOUND TO BE STYLISH.—Mrs. Dempsey— " Sure, an' Oi hear thot Mrs. Carroll is after gettin' a dayvorce." Mr. Dempsey—" Och f an' it's a divil she allus wor fer kapin' up wid th' fashions." AN EXPLANATION.—First Detective.—" There really isn't any evidence against him." Second Detective-.-" Why did you arrest him ? " First Detective—" Well—er there isn't any evidence against anybody else." FULLY QUALlFlED.—Practical Aunt: "Do you think you are qualified to become the wife of a poor man ? " Sweet Girl: "Oh, yes; it's all fixed 1 We are to live in a cottage; and I know how to make cottage pudding." THE GREATER BENEFACTOR. Teacher: "The inventor of pins did more for the world than the builder of the Pyramids. Why is that, Johnny ?" Johnny Thickhed : "Because, ma'am, you—er—er —can't bend a Pyramid and put it on the seat of • chair."

UNSCIENTIFIO.—First Arctic Explorer: "I have always considered Columbus a somewhat over- estimated man." Second Arctic Explorer: "Why ?" "First Arctic Explorer : "He dis- covered America the first time he went to look for it."

HIS SOLUTION.—Mrs. Vansook (at the children's party) : ".1 declare, little girls and boys of twelve stay up half the night nowaday " Mrs. Newly. blessed (absently) : "I suppose they acquire the habit while they are babies." COMMON HEREDITARY TRAIT.—" Doctor, what do you regard as the surest hereditary trait— that is, what peculiarity is most likely to be in. ?" "My observations lead me to believe that the desire to escape work is about the most common thing that people inherit." SAGE ADVlCE.—Gussie—" Bah Jove! Willy, where ye going ? " Willy—" Bah, Jove ! Gussie, I've a double engagement—first I'm going awound and awsk old Crimsonbeak law his daughtah's hand, and then I'm going awound and get some photos taken." Gussie—" Bah Jove! Wily, take a fool's advice, and get your photos taken first, yeh know 1" REDUCED CIRCUMSTANCES.—LittIe Girl: "Please give me a penny, ma'am. Mother is dead, and my father can't go out at night any more by the doctor's orders, and so can't earn any money." Benevolent Passer-by: "Can't go out at night? Why, what's your father's business ?" Little Girl: "He's a burglar, ma'am; and before he was laid up with bronchitis we used to live beautifully!" LAWYER : "Are you single ? " Female witness: " No." Lawyer: "Then you are a married woman I" Witness: "No." Lawyer: "So you are a widow?" Witness: "No." Lawyer: "But, my dear -madam or miss, you must belong to one of these classes. As what shall I put you down ?" Witness: "I am—an—engaged woman."

"My autograph? Delighted, I'm sure. Have you any preference as to its form ? " "If it is all the same to you, Mr. Jones, I should prefer it at the bottom of a cheque for fifty shillings, made to the order of Snip and Cuttum, tailors. You have the bill, I believe."

PBOVISIONAL.—A girl baby was brought to a clergyman to be baptised. He asked the name of the baby. "Dinah M.," the father responded. "But what does the M. stand for?" asked the minister. "Well, I don't know yet; it depends upon how she turns out." "How she turns out? Why, I do not understand you," said the minister. "Oh, if she turns out nice and sweet and handy about the house, like her mother, I shall call her Dinah May. But if she has a 6ery temper and a bombshell disposition like mine, I obeli call, her ' stiahwr • • Dinah AN Army officer tells an amusing story of an in- cident that occurred at Maidstone, many years ago, In the time of the old Cavalry depot. On a certain very foggy night there was complete silence, broken only by the voices of the sentries, who, at regular Intervals, passed the ueual word down the line. The officer woke up just as the usual watch was passing, and this was what he heard. First sen- try "Number one, and all's well." Then there was silence for a moment, and a voice called into the darkness, "Number Three, and all's Well, and Number Two's asleep." Before Number Pour could take up the thread of the preceedings, a voice, in which more than a susnicion of slumber S remained, cried hurriedly, " Number Two, and all's welt; aud Number Three's a liar 1" A ceRTAIN politician was once at a loss how to provide himself with a new pair of understandings, For bootmakers, in common with other tradesmen, absolutely refused him further credit. Eventually he hit upon an ingenious expedient. Going to one bootmaker, he ordered a pair of boots, to be paid for on delivery, and then, entering another shop, ordered a similar pair to be peal for in similar fashion. When the first pair of boots came home, the politician cried them on in the hall, and, find- ing that the right boot was a misfit, he sent it back to the shop for a slight alteration. When the second pair arrived he found fault with the left boot, and it was likewise sent back for altera- tion. He thus retained a pair of boots. In each case the messenger had been instructed not to leave the boots unless he received the money for them ; but he imagined naturally enough that there was no harm in leaving one boot. IN countries which are much visited by curious travellers everything becomes a show, from the natives' point of view. D. Seeman relates an observation of his own to this etiaet. "I suppose it must be in remembrance of any own educational training, and for the sake of comparing my .own lot as a boy with that of others, that I always 'find myself inquiring, with almost savage satisfaction, what punishments are iniitcted in the various coun- tries on ne'ar-do-weels. Can addressing one day my favourite questions to a schoolmaster at Cairo, he told me he gave the younr Egyptians the bastinado. 'I have often read of that,' I said, but have never seen it applied." Then you shall see it now,' he rejoined, and forthwith pro- ceeded to collar one of the biggest boys and indict the usual Oriental castigation. The boy helloed out tremendously, and I naturally inquired for what offence he was punished. 'Oh, no offence!' was the reply. I gave him the bastinado merely because you said you had never seen it applied. Of course I at once interceded, gave the boy two shillings for his pains, and the schoolmaster sixpence for his."
THE MOST NUTRITIOUS.

div.head: ' LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: ' LADIES' LETTER.

HY DEUR NELMS, In a very pretty blouse you might make the revers and collar of white silk or soft Oriental satin, stitched several times, and the little vest of tucked white chiffon. This could be made on a separate lining, so that you could change it for a vest of transparent ecru or fine black lace, to make a variety. It would not be necessary to tuck the silk, if it has stripes in it, but if you wished to do so you should make one small tuck in the centre of each black stripe. You had better have a waistband of drawn black satin or panne velvet, cut on the cross, but, if you wish to introduce any colour, you might have a collar-band and waist- band of drawn panne velvet in turquoise-blue, or any other colour that is becoming to you. You would find the silk looks much handsomer if you tucked it all over the bodice and sleeves on the black stripes, but perhaps you would think this too much trouble.

Touches of gold upon a gown are to be the height of fashion this winter. Gold webbing is used for many waist belts, and can be bought ready-made wit the addition of a handsome buckle in the froet one of the enamelled kinds, or of bronze, gilded and tinted. Gold braid is not cheap, and has a tiresome habit of tarnishing, but the merest sus- picion of it to form a band beneath the cuffs or an outlining upon a bolero suffices to lift an ordinary dress into the first rank of modishness.

Panne is aspiring to a fresh season. It composes the prettiest and most costly blouses, but in this connection too there are alternatives. For example, a spotted velvet is a delightful substitute, and was the fabric used in company with hussar blue cloth for a street gown. The spotted velvet was used for the boleto, which opened in front over a vest of gold tissue and cloth connected in alternate lines, and these with a gold tissue belt and tiny gold buttons on the bolero stamped the toilette with the hall-mark of success.

The size ot the fashionable toque gives a rather top-heavy look to a smart woman, especially if she is short in stature. It seems to be the very short- est who wear the largest and widest toques. II they could see themselves in outline without any of that partiality which is inspired by self-love, they would for ever after choose their headgear in better proportion with their own dimensions. It might also occur to them to view the matter objec- tively, and to reflect that it is a real inconvenience to passers-by in frequented streets to find a large hat jogging their elbows or on a line with their shoulders. Women run so tall nowadays that they share this inconvenience with men. A few under- sized, large-hatted women in a crowd can make a large number of persons uncomfortable. Still a great many of them in my opinion look smart.

A cheap and pr.-41# Aress can be made of spotted net with a (I.*.aped upper. skirt edged with a flounce el the rzat-orial, and an under-skirt entirely covered With narrow frills. The low, round bodice has a berth° of the frilled net, with a deep corselet belt of glace silk and a large rosette of the same on the left shoulder. This dress looks best in black without colour, but it is not amiss in white, with belt and shoulder-knot of rose-pitik, turquoise, or yellow glace. The sip worn under transparent gown of this sort must, of course, resemble silk to some extent, but there are many substitutes to be had which serve their purpose well, and cost but a few pence per yard. Black velvet has great possibilities before it this winter in achieving renown. It is much used for dinner gowns cut en princesse, with few trimmings or adornments beyond some rare lace on the corsage. Linen applique work continues to be very popular among those who are addicted to decora- tive stitchery, and a new notion for the adornment of a tea-cloth or table centre of white linen is to border it with a row of sunflowers cut out of yellow linen and laid close together at the extreme edge of the cloth. The petals of the flowers are button- holed round, and the centres filed in with an open lattice-stitch. The same notion can be carried out in a more expensive style by using cream silk or satin for the cloth and deep yellow velvet for the applique, the centres of the flowers having tiny paste diamonds dotted about them. For dress trimmings or coat facings appliques of bright- coloured velvet on biscuit, cream, or pale grey cloth are decidedly in vogue, and if home-worked their cost is less than half the shop price. The velvet designs are generally conventional and not too elaborate, and they are outlined, as a rule, with black cord. Velvet appliqué on cloth looks well mounted as blotting-nooks, wall-pockets, lamp-mats, foot-stools, and many other articles, and very small scraps of velvet can be most success- fully utilised in this way. Your loving JENNIE.

div.head: CHAPTER XII.
div.p: CHAPTER XII.
ROBERTSON'S AGENCY.

The candle found and lighted, Hester led the way through a labyrinth of corridors and passages. They did not attempt to go out through the front door by which Sybil had been admitted in the afternoon, but arriving in a great kitchen Hester unbolted a door that led into a small, stone-paved, roofed courtyard. From this opened another door, which had also to be unfastened, and they were at last in the open air. The night was very dark, and a fine, cold rain was falling. Sybil could only dimly see a path, and a high, black wall iith a gate, which Hester unlocked, and, passing through, they were free. "Thank Heaven the danger is over!" murmured Sybil, lifting her face almost joyously to the cold wind and drizzling rain. "Thank Heaven, indeed ! " echoed the other. "But the danger is not yet over, and it is only Heaven who knows when it will be. For where are we to go now that we have come so far ? I haven't a friend in the world; am d though I don't know so very much about your life I have heard enough of you to fancy that you have no friends either. If you had, the man who Planned this affair would not nave dared do what he has done—no, not even he, though he would dare a great deal. The only thing I know is to get as far away from here as possible. After that the future is all blank. I don't see what is to become of us, do you ?"

"No," said rybil,-"I don't see. But I think God must see, and I belieT,, that He will help. We can only do our best and hope." "You are a brave little thing. I wouldn't have thought you had so much in you. But you have more courage than I have, and if it hadn't been for you we should not have escaped at the last. When I saw my stepmother in the attic, where I had fancied we were safe as long as we cared to stay, I felt almost as if I were frozen for a moment, and it was you who broke the spell. I can take you out of this neighbourhood; after that you will have to decide everything for yourself." Beyond the gate in the wall they came into a long, open road, without a house to be seen in the darkness. .But this road they almost instantly deserted for a path that led over a rough stile across a sodden meadow. After a walk of a mile or more they came to the outskirts of a village, whose name Hester carefully refrained from mentioning. Not far away was a railway station, she said, but it would not be safe to venture there. Her ankle ached, but she was able to go further. Was Sybil of the same mind? Sybil was ready to do whatever was best; and so the two girls plodded on through the night and the rain. Sybil had never been out alone after dark Wore, but she was no longer afraid. After the horrors of that house of mystery by the river the great purple arch of sky seemed to hang above them like a benediction.

Hester's idea was to walk till daylight, aiming for another village (indirectly on the way to London) by such devious paths as to minimise danger of pursuit and discovery. Having reached their destination about the time that the village shops opened, Sybil (who still wore the hat and jacket in which she had set out from Mitchell- street) must take Hester's purse and buy her friend a hat and wrap of some sort. This done, and the new articles put on in a retired spot where Hester would wait for the purchase to be com- pleted, their appearance need not excite suspicion. Hester had in her possession several pounds, and they could afford to hire a fly, which would drive them a long distance to a railway station not likely to be watched.

!; "If anyone is lying in wait for us in London it will be at Waterloo Station," she explained to Sybil. "If we went by the straightest and best way we should arrive there, but by driving for about twelve miles, to the next county, we can come into town by way of Cannon-street, which is down in the City. And London, you know, is the best hiding-place in all the world." How she accomplished that long night journey on foot Sybil never knew. She grew light-headed with extreme hunger, and the road seemed to rise and fall before her like the waves of the sea. But the rain and the cool air were reviving, and, somehow, she was always ready to take just one step more. It was nearly eight o'clock in the morning when they reached the village of Wandell, and they had been walking for six or seven hours, Hester said. To Sybil it appeared twice that time, and she could hardly control her voice when, with the bare- headed Hester waiting in the covered porch of a :house to let, she walked into a small shop that was just opening and bought a cheap sailor hat. A . black cloth mantel was advertised as being for sale at half its original value, and this also she purchased for Hester. From the open door behind the shop came a comfortable fragrance of tea and frying bacon. The place was warm, too, and the sudden change of atmosphere made Sybil doubly conscious of her own misery. She was wet through and shivering with cold, so that her teeth chattered as she asked the price of the things she had bought and thanked the woman who sold them for the bchange.

"You do look cold," exclaimed the mistress of the house and shop. "I've but just had breakfast, and my husband hasn't finished his yet. The tea's quite hot, and there's plenty and to spare. Won't you have a cup ? " . Sybil longed to answer "Yes," but she could not bear to refresh her weary body while poor Hester waited and had nothing; so she wistfully thanked the woman and went out into the cold, raw morning with her parcel. Hester reported that no one had passed except some small boys, who had not noticed her standing behind the lattice of the narrow porch set far back from the road.

"We can go and have something to eat now," she said. "I am sick with hunger, and you must be far worse. There will be some little cheap restaurant in the village where cyclists stop for lunch and tea. They will give us coffee and a roll or an egg there I should think, early as it is." Half-an-hour later the girls felt like different beings. They had found such a place as Hester described, and to them the very inferior coffee and stale buns seemed the most delicious things they had ever tasted. Sybil's chilled blood ran warmly through her veins once more. Her heart was heavy for the death of the handsome, selfish man she had tried so loyally to love ; but she could not grieve for him with the passionate, consuming regret that, because he was her father, she would fain have felt. Youth triumphed over grief, and horror, and the effects of privation, exposure, and fatigue. Sybil had not been conscious before that life was sweet, though it held little of gladness ; but not the thought of having escaped a great danger, of coming out froin the cloud of Mystery and terror that had surrounded her in the old house by the river, set her pulses leaping. When she and Hester had finished their frugal breakfast they went in search of a fly, for which the elder girl shrewdly bargained with the proprietor. They were to drive to Stanton, in Kent., some twelve or fifteen miles away, and Hester was determined to make the journey as cheaply as possible. At last she was satisfied with the understanding arrived at and they set out, Sybil wrapped in a rug that had lain on the seat of the fly. Hester in the warm, dry mantel lately purchased, was compara- tively comfortable, despite the damp clothing underneath, but Sybil had looked pale and pinched and Hester had insisted on the rug. Though they were far away from the house by the river now, still the girls instinctively sat far back in the shadowy depths of the old vehicle which smelt of age and mustiness, and kept their eyes alertly fixed on the road as the horse jogged leisurely along. Many questions hovered on Sybil's lips, hut sho forced them back, for everyone over-stepped tho boundary of the promise she had been forced to make. She wished to know what Hester had heard of her before their strange meeting; why Hester had lived in the house by the river; what possible connection the life of the unknown "Ralph " might have with her father's and hers that he had wished to cut them short; and a hundred other things besides. But between Hester and herself the past was to be closed: they could only hold free com- munication regarding the future. At Stanton they left their fly at the railway station, where Hester, white-faced, eager-eyed, glanced about in veiled anxiety. But there was no one on the platform save themselves. A train for London was due in twenty-minutes—a slow one, since the early trains taking men to town in time for the business of the day were all gone.

Hester did not spealt out ner fears, but Sybil lcaew that her companion did not ,have an eau moment until they were seated in a third-class: compartment, moving with increasing swiftness out of the station.

"One more stage safely passed !" she exclaimed, with a deep sigh of relief. "I begin to be a little hopeful, although, knowing that man so well, I remember always that he will never cease to look for us until he has us held tight in the hollow of his hand again. If days pass, and still nothing happens, we must never let ourselves forget that at any moment the end may come!" She spoke with such earnestness, her great black eyes so dilated, her voice hushed to such intensity, that Sybil felt for an instant all the old spell of mystery from which she had broken free stealthily enfolding her. again. "What a dreadful life for us to live "she crieL "It would be like sleeping in a coffin at night, and wearing a shroud by day. Don't say that it must be like that. This horrible man will never find us —never."

"I hope not," Hester said, hesitatingly. "Once —only twenty-four hours ago—l would not have believed it if anyone had told me that I should feel towards him as I do. If I had not found something which he had written with his own hand, speaking of me as he really thought, I would have gone on being his dupe—thinking that, how- ever bad he might be, at least he loved me and would be true to me, while I was true to him. But we won't talk of him any more. Let us speak of ourselves. We have made up our minds that we are going to hide in London, far from any parts that we have ever seen or known before. But I have only three pounds left in the world, and you—"

- "I have not a penny," answered Sybil. "If it had not been for you, I could have done nothing." "We're even then," returned Hester; "for you saved me in the attic. And it hasn't cost much more for us two than it would for one alone—only the railway fare extra. We can live together in London for weeks on three pounds, if we're careful; and meanwhile, we must both look about for some- thing to do. You'll soon get tired of me as a chum, I know, for I'm not a lady like you." "Don't say that I " exclaimed Sybil. "It hurta me. lam a stranger in England, for I've lived abroad all my life nearly, till the last fortnight, and I shouldn't know what to do if I were left quite alone. Yet I won't be a burden on you. I've been thinking this morning of what I might do to earn a living. I often wanted to try it before, but father—poor, poor father !—would never allow it. I can speak French, and German, and Italian, as well as I can English; I can play and sing a little besides, and I think I ought to be able to teach. I could earn enough to live on, and pay you back all I owe you besides." "All you owe me!,' echoed Hester, with bitterness. "It's hardly more than a chance that you don't owe me your death. But there are lots of girls wanting just such places, and it might be months before you could get a situation. We can only live for a few weeks on what we have. It strikes me that neither you nor I can afford to pick and choose. And as for, a place to live—it ought to be one where there'll be the least risk of our being discovered, yet it should be not too far away from chances of getting work. I've been asking myself where his ways of life are least likely to lead him, and it seems to me that some- where near that big part of London that is called the City might be best for us. We could find lodgings within walking distance of houses where they employ girls in lots of ways—addressing envelopes, and factories where they make artificial flowers, and—oh, all sorts of things. We might get something to go on with, anyhow, till a bev€l. opportunity opened." • As they discussed ways and means, the train slowed into the big station at Cannon-street.

"We'll get out of this as quick as we can," said Hester, with the same restless glances she had given before leaving Stanton. "There isn't much danger that there can be anyone watching for us here; but who knows, when one has such an enemy as we have to deal with? I shall be happier when we are away." The two girls hurried out of the station, and did not stop walking at a rapid pace until, having turned several corners, they came to an unpreten- tious little 'restaurant.

"We'll buy two or three papers at this tobacconist's next door," said Hester, who took the lead here, by virtue of her superior knowledge, and then look at all the advertisements over another bun and some coffee.

Two or three newspapers Hester tossed asiao after an intent study of the advertising columns; but in the Daily Magnet her finger paused at last at a paragraph. "Here's the place for us to live, if it's as good as it pretends to be," she said.. "It's a lodging- house for young women employed during the day (which is what we hope to be)' and it's cheap, and in a street off the City-road. As for work, there's plenty advertised; but the worst of it is, there will be plenty after it, too. The best—or rather, tho most likely—thing I've come across yet, is a firm in London Wall who advertise for extra hands to address envelopes at the office. You're paid by the number you do in the day. We'll go there first, and try our luck. Afterwards will be time to see about the lodgings."

Sybil began t7o feel as if the only thing she was physically able to do, was to lie down and fall into a heavy, dreamless sleep, forgetful of all her mis- fortunes. But she would have died rather than confess her weakness to Hester. It was Hester's, money on which she must subsist until he could got work to earn her own living; and the sooner that work could be found, the more thankful would she be.

So, weighed down'by a weariness almost beyond bearing, she struggled to her feet with a wan little smile, and went whither Hester led. She saw the busy streets of the City as if through a haze, and the roar of constant traffic was like the sound of the sea in her ears. If it had not been for Hester, she would have been run over by a great dray on one of the crossings, for the noise and the turmoil of horses and carts and vans and omnibuses con- fused her; she had never been in the midst of such a scene before.

"Look here, we must decide on what names we are to take," Hester exclaimed, stopping at the door of a high building. "This is the place where we're going to apply for work. What are you going to call yourelf ? " "Can't I keep my own name?" asked Sybil, miserably. "Surely there can't be any danger of our being tracked to a place like this." Hester looked at the beautiful, weary little face with a strange expression in her big black eyes. "You can't understand what I mean, and I don't want you to understand; but if you were anyone except Sybil Wade you wouldn't be in danger any- where," she said, enigmatically. "As it is, you are in danger everywhere. And you must begin even to think of yourself as someone else." "My head aches so, I can't think of a name," answered Sybil. "I can't make anything seem of much importance just now. It will be different to-morrow—perhaps." "I'll think up a name for you, when I decide on one for myself," said Hester. "All you will have to do, is to listen when I Mention it, and answer to it afterwards. Now let me take a good look at you, before we go up, and see if you arc quite presentable to ask for a situation." Her bright eyes dwelt critically upon Sybil. "You are pretty enough for anything," she pro- nounced. "I thought yesterday, in front of that house in Bloomsbury, when you came out, and I saw you first, that you were the prettiest thing I had ever seen hi my life, arvi you seemed such a tender, dainty little creature, my heart stood still at the thought of bringing harm upon you. You're just as putty to-day, though you look almost ready to faint, and anybody with eyes car see it is only pluck that is keeping you up. But your frock is awfully pulled about. That was my beautiful stepinother•t work on the attic stairs last I suppose, though I've been too busy to notice it before. The skirt's torn down from the Ivaist ; but, luckily, your jacket covers that pretty well. I wonder where you got that bit ripped so cleanly out, just above the hem ?" "I. seem to remember catching it somewhere last night," said Sybil, "and pulling it free in a hurry; perhaps I shall recall how I did it by-and-bye." She was to recall both time and place in a way she little dreamt of now. At present, she did not care, and was merely anxious to go up the long flights of stairs to the third floor, where 10bertson's Eclair Addrsssing Agency was situated. Only to get the ordeal over ! She could look no further than that into the future.

At the top of the third flight of stairs the name the two girls wished to find confronted them in black letters on white. Hester tapped at the doer so adorned, and, with a businesslike air of being no amateur in such matters, walked boldly in without waiting for permission. Sybil followed, binT;hing hotly. She had hardly realised before exactly what she would have to face, untl she crossed the threshold of a small outer office, to meet the supercilious stare of a man who at ooposite the door. at a lame. roll-topped desk.

Sybil qsexcled at once that he was a natant man. He was approaching middle age, and had the countenance of a bulldog, without its faithfulneni or honesty. Even the young, inexperienced girl, who had learnt go little of human nature in her seventeen years, felt that here was a man who would delight in abusing his authority, rejoice ja tyrannising over those weaker than himself. At another end of the small, stuffy room, wine' was heated by a paraffin stove, sat a girl tan,„.ing busily away at a typewriting machine. 'I entrance of the two new-corners did not intelrruP her work, but she glanced up over the machint and with one look seemed to take in every detals of their appearance. She had a hard, sharp foe' surrounded by quantities of frizzy hair of 110 particular colour, and as her slanting grey eyes lit upon Sybil Wade's beautiful features, a jeal°u4 antagonistic gleam shot through them. "We've come in answer to your advertisement; which we saw in the Daily Magnet this morning, said Hester. "Ah I" The man at the desk deigned to obsern her, lifting his eyes from a letter in his hands, am' dropping them again at once, as if she were .9 thing of no importance. "You are rather late ol applying. I think we have all the assistance we at present; but if you choose, you can both she" me a specimen of your writing. Miss Monstanee:_ some paper here, if you please. Now, you c,an boto write your names and addresses." A quick glance passed between the girls, e°6 unobserved by Miss Monstance, the young. wt'ulani with the typewriter, who maliciously noted there seemed to be something rather queer in tha'
_ _. quarter. ot As Sybil took the pen that was offered he,r, 4ito 0. knowing what to write, a door opened, asa "" men came into the room.
(To be continued.)

The Prince and Princess of Wales are entertaining at their Nirfolk home, their customary series or boase parties, but more quietly than Would have been the case bad the Court not been in mourning. The shooting at Sandringham is extr, may good this year, and besides pheasants there are a great many partridges on the estate. The Princess is happily looking stringer, and in tetter spirits than has been the case for same time past, and Princess Victoria appears tar less deficit:: thur she did a year ago. Very little formliity is observed at Sandringham, by the Prince and Princess of. Wales, who are an ideal host and hostess.

Prince ad Princess Charles of Denmark have arrived at Appleton House, where the Princess 12pea to remain. It is no secret that Her Royal Highness detests Denmark and many of her husband's relatives, and that she would be only to glad to settle clown at Appleton, which is within a stone's throw of Sandringham Howe. N)w there are three lives between the aged King ot Denmark and Prince Charles. it is just possible that Her Ryal Highness will not again be called upon to leave, for auy length of time, the friends, home and country sne loves so well.

The appointment of Lord Cbesham, as master of the Queen's staghounds, came as a pleasant s.urprise. He has had considerable experience with foxhounds, and was for eight years maatel of the Meester hunt, besides being wel!-known in the Shires. He took am active part in raising the Imperial Yeomanry for South Africa, where he is now. Lord Churchill meanwhile filling his place. Curiously enough, the new master's arms very appropriately include three stags' heads and dexter sun- ported by a back. As wet weather interfered with th- opening fixtures, sport so far has been very moderate. The state of the ground undoubtedly accounts for ,soine of the casualties already reported from the tunting field.

Sir Redvers Buller, after being feed in his native county, is to be entertained by the Devonians in 1.,•:43- don at a banquet at the Hotel Cecil, on the 30th inst. There wilt be a presentation of an illuminated address, and ladies are invited to join in the welcir.e. Lady Audrey Buller, who has been much gratified by the en- thepiastic reception of her hustat.d cn his return home, will be present. General Buller will return to his duties at Alderehot early next year, and in the meanwhile he has to face a formidable tiet of banquets and entertain- ments to be given in his honour. Thl gallant General is no doubt pleased with the p )pular enthisiasm with which he has been everywhere received, but it is no se^,ret that he regards these festivities with c-)risiOerable apPiehension. It was not given to Sir Redvers, any more than to other men, to invariably command succe Si but he always upheld the Lest traditions of the Army and among them may perhaps be reckoned his strong disinclination to be " tekised over."

The are responsible for the very fascinating wavy brims which are seen in the newest beaver, and felt headgear, for the vagueness of the undulating, battered brims of the khaki hats inspired leading milliners with the idea of producing a *arming effect. haw-By without the necessity of tb6 wearer going through a Ampaign similar to that in wh.ch the men distirguisheci themselves so splendidly. The predomina- ting colcur in millinery at the present moment, is red, another feminine compliment to the Army. Grey with a pinkish tinge is also much worn, so is petunia, which is half red, half violet. Cherry cr lour is seen too, tut is too crude, for the gen eratity of comolexions. Tea gowns have never becc me really popular with any but the wealthy classes, and yet, for home wear, no garment combines so many distinct advantages. It suits both old and young, it is graceful, and comfortable, and can be quickly put on, as it consists of but one piece, which being complete in itself requires no accessories to finish it. To those who regard it as an unattainable luxury, it may he suggested that half-worn silk day, or evening gowns lend themselves most accom- rnodatiegly to a really smart r-appearance as tea gowns. With the addition of lace, velvet, panne, or chiffon, an elegant garment may be evclved, one calaulated to prove a boon and a blessing to its possessor. Bead chains are among the latest novelties. Thr.so any wc-ccran can tl.-ret,d fr herself,adding tasselled ends. They are passed two or three times round the neck, and the tassels are featured to the bodice. Oriental beads have the preference, but amber, malachite, mummy Venetian, turquoise, and cut crystal are all worn. Pretty eyeglass chains are made of a single row If gold beads. The fortunate possessors of old paste buckles can now display them to advantage on the wide waisthelt of satin or velvet, wbich Giv g a moot becoming Doish to a Fmart dress.

Among the Roman Catholics, the priests are forbidden to smoke in public. The Pope does not Erni:he, but he takes snuff, and several of his predecessors were great snorters. One however, never looks for the smell of tete.cco about a clergyman, and whenever it is met with, it is generally the 'object of remark, which would pass unnoticed in other people. For if the car declines to move, In spite of all persua,ions, It offers me a chance to prove My patience. Or if my angry passions rise Bet ond the utn3est bearing, It berves to give me exercise In swearing. Despite the foolish critics then, I've proved in style judicial A motor car is always bene- ficial. U.S. BRIGGS.

the town. I think, also, that the Parr Hall might be more utilized on Saturday nights by the Corporation for popular recreation than it has been recently. Such works as these are a healthful and worthy line to follow; and all classes could join in them, and I commend them as a true use of the " increase "God has given To my thiiiking, it is a hopeful feature of our present town life, that people are getting to see that municipal work can be well cared for on its on merit and apart from party poltics. Macaulay speaks of the way in which in ancient Rome "none were for a party, but all were for the State." The sooner a spirit of that order becomes dominant in all our towns and cities, the better, in my judgment, it wilt be for the couutry. Our political and ecele,iastical differences have kept us too long and too far apart. For myself, I long more and more for the time when we can succeed, not in sinking conscientious beliefs and convic. tions, whether political or rsligious, hut in crediting one another with entire honesty of purpose, and with one : desire deeper and higher and broader than all others, namely, to promote the general well-toeing of the com- munity and the nation. Will it not be well for us mutually to concede one another'a patriotism ? Surely that can never be the monopoly of any party, or any sect. Will it not be well to believe also in the sincerity of each other's religious convictions, without trying to assume that true religion can only be found in any one creed or church? We are all called to be servants of one another, and to live in friendship and brotherhood with ore another. The supreme earthly cauQe that should hind us together is the cause of the welfare of the people. Surety no work can be nobler, because it is so all inclusive. The town couocillor, and the guardian of the poor, and the minister and teaeher of religion, have alike a Divine ministry. " The powers that be," as we reminded each other last year, " are ordained of Gad." The ordination is splendid ! Called of God to serve Him in serving the cominunity dud called of God now, in Warrington, by reason of such providential increase, awl in view of the near dawn of a new cen— tury, to better and fuller service than ever T. Let us reader the uustinted ;urine° that our God demands, and strive to make the town where Providence; has put the better for our life in it.

div.head: MAYOR'S SUNDAY.
div.p: MAYOR'S SUNDAY.
Visits to the Wycliffe and
Parish Churrthes.

In accordance with usual custom, the Mayor and Cor- Poration attended divine sntvice in their official capacity 011 Sunday. In the morning, they proceeded to Wycliffe ~„ ‘;',?ngregational Church, where the Mayor's Chaplain .(,nev John Yonge) preached. At night, the service at ‘ne Parish Cnurch eras attended. The pulpit was occu- Ited by the Rev. Canon Willis. The weather was die- OntlY unfavourable for a procession through tee streets „IA nevertheless a large number responded to the °mayor's invitation to accompany him. The procession each occasion was similar to those of previous years. 't was beaded by the Volunteer Cyclist Com- lz/anY and the transport section, numbering between .10 and 40 men ; then came the band and bugle band, 1..1e. Volunteers (250 strong under the direction of the di esutant), members of St. John's Ambulance Associa- a`leni the police under the directiou of Inspector Taylor, he mace and sword bearers, the Mayor (Alderman Roberts), who had the Town Clerk en his right, and .ahe Chaplain (the Rev. John Yonge) on his loft. Mr. Itobert Pierpoint walked with the Deputy-Mayor (Alder- Man James Fairclough). They were followed by the ilderinen, Councillors, public officials, magistrates and leading townsmen. At Wycliffe Congregational Church, a special musical tlngramtne had been arranged. The choir sang the an- them "0 come let 49 worship" (Mendelssohn), the solo Part belie.; efficiently sung by Mrs R H Pearson. The Volunteer bind accompanied the singing of the first QYnito and also the National A.nthem(with altered second 'Verse by the Dean of Rochester). Mr W H Payton, Mus. -Hee presided at the organ with his usual ability. The Rev J Yonge preached an able discourse. WELCOME TO THE CORPORATION. Prefacing his sermon, the Mayor's Chaplain said "It Ismy honourable privilege, in behalf ot our Wycliffe People, to offer respectful and cordial welcome to this 'very representative gathering of the officials and the People of this town. It can hardly need to be said, but I.t.ehould not go without saying, that this church re- -3°lnes in the re-election of Mr Alderman Roberts as mayor of Warrington; and it is glad that the distinc- tion of being the first mayor of this now county borough should have fallen to his lot. We are glad also that so many of the Council and townspeople generally have come with him to this service in the house of prayer to Which he belongs. Perhaps it may be allowed me 1° refer in a passing word to the exceptional Character of the municipal year that has just Closed, It has proved to be a time in which the duties and responsibilities of our public men have been very considerably increased. Probably nut" Mayor, in any dreams of office he may have had in the Past, little supposed that office would come to him in a time so momentous and exacting. But it is a satisfaction to the town that both his Worship and those Who have shared the burden with him have shown them- eelves so entirely equal to the occasion. The year has brought its own powerful appeals upon the patriotic de- Votion and generous beneficence of all classes. Whatever difference in opinion may have existed concerning the war in South Africa, there can have been none respect- ing the devotion of our Warrington Volunteers who offered for active service, and there can have been none respecting the duty of Warrington people making generous provision for the wives and families alike of Reservists and Volunteers. It is only due to the town generally to say that the ameunt of money that has been so freely given. not least by any means by the working classes, is infinitely to the general credit. And when it Is remembered further that the appeal for relief of the suffering millions in India, came contemporaneously with the appeal for help for our soldiers, it is additional satisfaction to know that the town has nobly responded also to that appeal, raising even more money in its behalf than for the last Indian famine when no other demand Was made upon public beneficence. Many gloomy predictions were uttered that the pressure of these extraordinary claims would cause the funds of Churches and benevolent institutions to suffer. So far I as my knowledge goes, at least in Warrington that has not been the case. This is a fact which seems to say that when people once get into the way of giving, they get to like it. There is greater luxury in it than in our Moods of SeVere and too selfish economy we sometimes Suppose. It is perhaps well also to make one more allusion of kindred nature. The Guardians of the War- rington Union are to be congratulated upon the C3lll- - and opening of the new infirmary at the Work- house. The admirable provision that is new made there for the treatment and comfort of the sick and destitute Poor is a noble step in true progress, and deserves general and cordial recognition. THE :MUNICIPAL MOTTO. Passinc, now from those incidental references, Suffer flee to invite your brief consideration to the subject I have been led to select. The choice of a text is often One of the greatest difileulties of a preacher, and speci- ally so whe'n occasion has special character. It has Occurred to me, however, that we might find a very amt- lele and timely theme suggested by the motto that is Inscribed upon the arms of the borough. Probably only a "tY small minority of Wareington people is aware that such a municipal motto is in existence. But, as you will see from the coat of arms printed upon your Service paper this morning, three Latin words are Inscribed thereen—" Deus dat Incrementum "—which Peing translated is seen to mean, " God giveth the I ,Dlnere‘Se." The words are taken from St. Paul's First 'epistle to the Corinthians, 3rd chapter, and seventh 'verse. I think it is manifest that the words form an tzceedinely apt and significant motto for a growing, e2tDandintse, and thriving community. They are a fitting , -ecugnitiorh increase, the pro- Inui.er of all true progress, the origin of all real pros- Pity. That such a"motto should have been chosen as the motto for this borough reflects considerable credit Upon those who made the selection. HOW THE MOTTO WM SELECTED. was a little Curious to discover how this choice had been arrived at, and also by whom it was made. I made enquiry, therefore, of the Town Clerk, and he has enabled me to relate the following interesting particulars. It anPears that when the armorial device for the borough Was being first desiened, two of the most prominent rwnsmen nf the day set themselves the task of discover- ing suitable motto. These two men were Mr. Beamont, Who was the first Mayor, and Mr. Fitchett-Marsh, who Was the firs' Town Clerk. In the year of the incorpora- tion. 1847. 53 years'ago, these gentlemen spent a large ICI-lout-It of lime on this matter. On their first confer- :nne they did not succe.d to their satisfaction, and so `,lles' arranged a meeting for the next morning, when `ht'Y would come to the final decision. When they so rn(tt • each of them took from his pocket a paper upon Which he had written his suggestion for a motto.' enriously enough, both had laid hold of the same scrip- tural sentence, which, of course, being tor the heraldic Purpose in view, they had rendered into Latin. But .., ey had each set the Latin words in a different order. Beamont'a surestion was, " Dat Deus Incremee- t.o en. Mr. Fitehett-Marsh's arrangement was "Dens dat Incrementum." In the first instance, Mr. Beamont's Setting was adopted, and you may see it so inscribed in the stonework over the principal entrance to the Market In 1897, however, when a new coat of arms was obtained for the town, our present Town Clerk adopted !de. form suggested by his first predecessor in office, and - therefore stands now, "Deus dat Incrernentum,' hay; • .ng oeen reeently so carved in the stonework of th., eiew police buildings. "God giveth the inereaie."

div.head: SERVICE AT THE PARISH CFIURCEL
div.p: SERVICE AT THE PARISH CFIURCEL

At the service held in the Parish Churcn in the even- ing, the Rector preached from the text : " The zeal of Tame house bath eaten rile up." St. John II part of the 17ch verse. At toe outset he con- gratulated tee Mayor upon his re-election. They all believed it, he said, to be a deserved honour for ability, energy, impartiality, and devotion of interest in all that concerned the welfare of the town. Might he also say that they congratulated themselves upon having such a Mayor at such an important time as this, when they read from the Mayor's address in the papers, there was so much to be done. They had confi- dence that by God's help he would be able to do it. Turning to the subject of his discourse the Rector spoke of great national sins, and what would be Christ's attitude with regard to them were He on earth. He dealt first with the sin of drunken- ness. He had before him, he said, the final report of her Majesty's Commissioners, issued last year. It told them that half the crime, halt the poverty, and a great, part of the misery in the country was due to drunken- ness. He had before him a map of England, divided in- to counties, and shaded in different degrees according to the number of offences committed in each couet,t from 150 or leas offences for every 100,000 people to 1,000 for every 100,000. They would see (showing the m tp) that three counties were marked black. Th6y were Nor- thumberland, Durham, and Lancashire. They must not live in a fool's paradise. There was much, indeed,to be thankful for, but there was much, indeed, to lament. He asked them what would be Christ's attitude in re- gard to this. Would He say that the whole traffic in drink was utterly bad from beginning to end ? Would Ile sweep away all the breweries and puhlic-houses from the face of the earth ? If he (the Rector; read Holy Scripture aright, he thought not. Although God hated ' the abuse he did not say the use of strong drink was wrong. He (the Reece) would point out the line be thought should be taken. He should provide all kinds of counter-attractioes, and at the same time make crr- tain restrictions. In this town the licences were in the proportion of one to 300 of the population. Competent authorities said that the proportion should be one to 1,000 of the population in the town and one to 500 in the country. Secondly, he would restrict the hours. What healthy man needed to drink strong drink at six o'clock in the morning? He would say that public-houses should be open from twelve to two at the dinner-hour and seven to nine at the supper-hour. Why should houses be open, at all times of the day for drinking and tippling ? A man only ruined his health by drinking at all times. On Sunday he would have public houqes open for one hour at mid-day, half-past twelve to half-past one, and one hour at night, from eight to nine and no more. The next restriction he would wish was that there should be the power to arrest for simple drunkenness—a perfectly impartial arrest for every man, whatever his position, if he were found drunk. Lastly, he would have no music and dancing licences, and no back doors. Why should a man b ashamed to go and get what was necessary? If be went for his dinner or supper beer he need not go to the back door. A hundred and fifty millions of money was spent in drink last year. Two-thirds of the amount sold was consumed by the working classes. The population was 40,000,000 and the working classes numbered 30,000,000. Out of £150,000,000, £100,000,000 was spent by the working classes. To turn from drunkenness to immoral- ity, he was speaking to a man of great experieace and in a high position on this subject, and he said "Thank God immorality is not one of the great sins of this town." So far as open immorality went, he the Rector) believed him. But a clergyman saw a great deal that other people did not see. Many who came to be married did not come as they should. There was much in regard to immorality that was not right in the sight of God. He referred in conclusion, to the misuse of the Lord's day. Look, he said, at this crowded church. Why were they there? Was it solely for the worship of God ? Would they be there if there was no special attraction ? There were many who lay in bed in the morning, went for a walk in the afternoon, and attended church in the evening when there was a bright and beautiful service There should be a Lord's moan- ing and afternoon, as well as evening. At the conclusion of the service the congregation sang the National Anthem.

div.head: Established 1849.
div.p: Established 1849.
WARRINGTON'S PROSPEROUS GROWTH.

Manifestly, that was a very timely as well as seemly recognition of the favouring Providence of God which, 53 years ago, had so endowed Warrington with prosper- ous growth as to enable it to take rank as a municipal borough. The population at that time, so far a I can ascertain,was about 24,000. The general appearance of the town (not any too fascinating even yet) must have been then very much less 60, for the late Rector, Mr. Quekett, has told us in his auto-biography what terrible"depression" Gime upon him on his firs: sight of it in 1854. But at th- date of the incorporation,the town was beginning to "shake itself from the dust," and to aim at better things. Since those days, the introduction of new and extensive industries, involving the establishment of large works, and the coming into the town of large numbers of workers have caused rapid extensions and widespread growth. Its commercial prosperity has steadily increased. Warrington now sends its varied commodities and macufactures t) all parts of the world. The enterprise of its people is winning natural and legitima:e con- quests. Its boundaries have been repeatedly advanced. lea population has consequently increased from 24,000 to 64,000. And now during the municipal year just closed the town has been elevated to the enhanced position, and augmebted dignity, but also to the greatly extended responsibiliAes, of a county borough. In view of all this growth, extension and development, it will appear to us, I think, that the municipal motto is finding yet greater and more striking appropriateness, so that it may well compel the tnoughc of all intelligent and ' earnest citizens," God giveth the increase."

div.head: LESSON OF THE TEXT.
div.p: THE LESSON OF THE TEXT.

Now, as we have seen alrealy, these worth were first used by the Apostle Paul. When he addressed them to the Christians at Corinth, he gave in so doing, a charac- teristic illustration of the true greatness of his nature Paul had humanly speaking been the founder of that church at Corinth. He had gone there as a Missionary of Jesus Christ. By the boldness and grace of his message, the courage and de- votioa of service,he had won t 3 the faith of Caristianity a number of the Corinthian people. The church in their midst was therefore one of his successes as a Minister of Christ. But now, when he wrote this letter, he is c areful to make it plain that he had no right to be re- garded by the converts as though he or his colleagues, were their leader and bean. " Mao then," he asks, "is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers (servants) by wnoss agency ye believed (or, were led to faith) as the Lord gave to every man. I have planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase ! So then, neither is he that planteth anything, nor he that watereth, but God that giveth the increase." Man is;nothing wicnout God. That was Paul's thought. Tnere we have defined and stated a great fact and principle, of which illustrations are numerous. In Paul's use of them, he is referring to the world of nature. In agriculture, horticulture, husbandry of every kind, it is man's part to cultivate the soil,to sow and plant, to tend, protect, and nurture, the various fruits and produce of the earth. His diligence, intelli- gence, enterprise, outlay, are all necessary in order to successful and prosperous result. But, after all that has been contributed the " increase" is of God. It is according to the laws which have been established by His power, His wisdom, and His will. Apart from His good pleasure. without the concurrent operation of His infinite, and supreme and beneficent power, the " increase" would nor come. Thus we are faced by this truth that expansion, development, progress, success, prosperity, whereinsoever they are true, right,and good, an the gifts of God. Too often that is not recognised. Sometimes it may be even disbelieved and denied. But disbelief and deaial do not constitute disproof. Admit the existence, and supremo sovereignty of a beneficent God and the faith expressed in this word of Paul is in- evitable, "Every good gift and every perfect gilt is from above, and cometh down from the Father of light." " A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven." This is true in the personal lives of men. It is true in the growth of a community. I; is true in. the expansion of an empire. In all these various realms all that is good is from God. It is" God tha:. civeth the increase."

DEPENDENCE UPON GOD FOR ALL TRUE BLESSING. Need it be said, my friends, how it would tend to the elevation and purification of all departments of lif.i, if his great and fundamental fact could be better realised? ersonal life would be redeemed from much that im- pairs its honour, and happiness, and prosperity, if we could always remember our absolute dependence upon God for all true blessing ; and if we could be led by that recollection to such character of life and conduct as can be fully crownei with His favour. But, whet,. in His goodness, God has "given the increase," what then ? What is " increase " given for ? Is it to be merely taken and received ? Is it to be regarded as a merely selfish possession ? Does it bring with it no duties, impose no new responsibilities ? Does it create no additional opportunities, and invite, even compel, to no fresh enterprises? We all condemn the individual who,—as his riches increase,—simply boards them, stows them away, fails to make that true use ot them which reason,—ti say nothing of philanthropy, and religion, demands. A more truly despicable character can hardly exist than that of the man who grows richer every year, and yet, neither in his own person, or family, or com- munity, makes no seemly use of the wealth that has come to him. Similarly,—a community which achieves, or is granted, manifold and various" increase" needs to realise that such "increase " means augmented duty, enlarged responsibility, expanded opportunity, and re- doubled enterprise. That,as I understand it, is the case with Warrington to-day. And it is to that phase of our common and corporate life that,ty the motto borne upon our Municipal Coat of Arms, I would call the attention of Warrington people by this address. "God giveth the increase." Since Ile has so bestowed it.—what is His i meaning in the gift, and what should be our purpose n its possession ?

div.head: MISSION OF THE CHRISTIAN PULPIT.
div.p: THE MISSION OF THE CHRISTIAN PULPIT.

Many things have been well pointed out lately by the Mayor and others about the additional powers possessed by the town now that it has become a " County " Boroueh. Now, I do not desire to enter any domain which can properly be considered outside the province of the pulpit, or beyond the privilege of the chaplaincy I have the honour to hold. Nor am I about to offer any counsels such as could only rightly come from a munici- pal expert. But, Ido not sympathise, with the view which some seem to hold as to the mission of the Christian pulpit. Tha: mission has been very vaguely, and very inaccurately, defined as being discharged by a presentation of tho "simple Gospel," whatever that may be supposed to mean. The belief which has guided me throughout my ministry as a preacher, is this : that the Christian pulpit has for its theme whatever affects the general welfare, whether of individuals or communities. No, my friends, the truth of the matter lies here : the pulpit has a sphere as wide as humanity. The Gosixi of the Lord Jesus Christ, whose own personal mintetry on earth was directed to alerfti physical, as well as spiritual, welfare, has teaching to give upon all the affairs of actual life. Whatever tends to make men healthier, purer, happier, and more truly prosperous is therefore a legitimate theme for the pulpit, and, it is a fitting theme to be wisely discussed especially on a Sunday like this. Will you, therefore, allow me to say, especially in view of our extended municipal powers sad opportunities, that one great pre- ' !eat next in our town is an increase of intelligent interest in the general welfare upon the part of every- body ? Ido not sileak now specially to, and certainly not " at" the members of the Council ; but I say this to an audience which is so generally representative of 'the town. the real welfare of the town is not in the 1 exclusive care of the Council, it is in the keeping of the town itself; consequently, what is wanted is the growth of a true and healthy public opinion among hll classes. All our people need to look upon the duties of citizenship atl Christian duties, even as religious responsibilities. In seeking to improve the physical conditions and sur- roundings in which our population live, we are fulfilling the will of God. In promoting the order, an(f cleanli- ness, and healthfulness of houses and streets; in amend- ing or destroying insanitary dwellings ; in exercising peculiar care concerning the housing of the peorer classes ; in making it possible for fresh air and sunlight to penetrate and purity localities that are ill-drained, close, dark, and dismal ; in providing wherever possible, open spaces for the healthful recreation of the people ; even in devising rational and elevating pleasures for those who cannot provide them for themselves ; in ways such as these the people of the town can combine to Promote the welfare of the town. I was delighted to hear the Mayor's proposal on Friday respecting the future use of the ground now occupied by the present police build- ings. An open space there would be a vast and hesiltb- ful improvement, and might lead the way to further amendment of what is now a very melancholy part of
THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, NOVE \I BE It 16, 1900.
A WIFE'S MISCONDUCT.
Divorce Case from Warrington.

In the Dtvorce Court, yesterday week, efore Sir Francis Jenne, president, Luke WeDings, v. in -Irawer, of 13, Jolley-street, Warrington, tu .d tor a divorce from his wife, Annie Wellings, who at the time et the pre- sentation of the petition was residing in Dough, Isle of Man, but at the present time is reAding in Wart ington. —Mr. J. C. Priestley, inatrueted by Mr. Arthur Browne, appeared for ths petititiner, and Mr. Biytord !or the res- pondent. The petitioner stated the t he and re;pondeut were married in 1895 in the Unitarian Chapel, Cairc-street, Warrington. For theArst 18 mouths of thetr Inarrd life they lived very co-nfortably tt.gether. The rest on- dent then contracted drinking habits, which contir.ued until he was so tired of it that he left her on the 3cd of October, 1899. Subsequently an arrangement between them for payment of alimony was made by the Hey, W. ,IL Drummond, and he (petitioner) continued to pay until be discovered that the respondent had ben guilty of adultery. Be filed his petition on June 23,d. Eli, I alleged three acts of misconduct which would be proved lby independent witnesses.—Cross-earimined : Be denied cruelty towards the respondent. Evidence for the petitioner was given by Frederick Samuel Percival, wire drawer, and George Clarke,' time•keeper, as to witnessing misconduct on the part of 1 the respondent with an unktown man on October 5 h, 1899. _

Elizabeth Bond, a neighbour of the respondent, spoke to havine seen misconduct on the morning of September 19th, 1900. Petitioner gave evidence regarding the third act of miPconduct on September 30th. P.C. Boxendate, if the W.rrington Po'ice Force, was present to corroborate this statement, but it was not considered necessary to call him. It was admitted that the respondent had given way to drinking habits. The respondent was sworn an I denied the allegations of misconduct. She gave evidence of numerous acts oi cruelty by the petitioner. The Rev W El Drummond gave evidence to the effect that on the morning after the alleged misconduct on September 30th the petitioner had a conversation with him with reference to his wife's conduct, and told him that he had not actually seen improper conduct take place. When the petitioner left his wife on September 30th he (witness) sent the respondent to some friends in the Isle of Man for the purpose of trying to reclaim her from her drinking habits. In answer to the President, _ _

Witness stated that he did so entirely on his Own authority. The petitioner called to see him on a subse- quent occasion and asked him what he bad done with his wife or where be had sent her to. Witness further stated that the petitioner had not acted with the kind- ness he might have dove towards the respondent. A letter was produced written by Mr Drummond to the petitioner in June in which he stated he believed the best possible course bad been followed under the cir- cumstances.

The President in summing up said he did not con- sider it necessary t) go into the third charge of miscon- duct, inasmuch as the first charge had been proved be- yond all doubt. The next point for tim to settle was whether the petitioner had been guilty of cruelty to the respondent Be was quite satisfied that not a single act of cruelty bad been proved. In letters which the respondent had written to the petitioner after he left her,she spoke of him having treated her with every kind- ness and expreesed regret for having given way to drink. Two specific sets of cruelty had been alleged,but neither had been proved, and even if they had he did not think they were of such a nature as to prevent him giving the petitioner the relief he asked for. He therefore granted a decree nisi.

Mr. Bay ford stated that the petitioner bad now been reclaimed, and he asked his Lordship to make an order for alimony. His Lordship declined, saying : I must say in all my experience of this court, I have never known a drunken woman reclaimed.

went on to speak of the various Chestian agencies em- ployed for the conversion of the people, and gave a very Ii t re,ting account of preaclinig work in the mission haUs, the village evangelizttion, and the work of the medical missionaries. Speaking iocidentally of the use ot opium, he said that the responsibility for the whole- sale poisoning by opium of mallow+ of Cuinese people wr.s upon the English nation for enforcing it upon them Irom India. In speaking of the work of the Christian Chinch he said it was growing from year to year and there was every reason for them to have confidence in the missionaries out there. He appealed for the sym- pathy, prayer and libemiity of Christian people. Referr- ing to the success which had already attended. the work in China, he said there were over 100,000 native Chris- tians and thrre were hundreds of thousands besides who weie on the point of deciding for Christ. On the motion of Alderman Shaw Green, second, d by Mr atyward, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman and Mr Tomlinson.

div.head: FOREIGN MISSIONARY MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: FOREIGN MISSIONARY MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
Anniversary at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.

The Foreign Missionary Anniversary in connection with Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church was celebrated on Sunday and Monday. The minister (Rev C H Hocken) himself a returned missionary from India, has succeeded in arousing additional interest in foreign missions and the amount raised has consequently increased in recent years The inclement weather and the Mayoral visit to the churches interfered with the attendance on Sunday, but, nevertheless the collections were slightly in advance of the preceding year. The preacher at the morn•ng service was the Rev C llHocken. In the afternoon a novel juvenile meeting was held, when eight young people in native costumes (Chinese, Burmese, Hindu and African) spoke and sang native songs, Mr !lambley, of Southport, presided. A people's missionary meeting took piaci:3in the evening. Mr B Wadsworth presided at the organ. Collections made for the mission funds amounted to £l4 03 SJ, The missionary meeting was held on Monday evening. Councillor Brough presided, and was supported on the platform by the Revs W S Tomlinson, from China (deputation), 0 H Hocken and T Bishop, and Masers J W Hayward, J.P., W Parkinson, and .Tames Horton. Captain W A Savage, who was expected to preside, was unable to be present, and sent a contribution of £5 to the collection.

The Rev. C. H. HOCKEN presented the annual report, which showed that the annual income of the society for the year 1899, including le acies, was £132,690. After all expenbes had been paid £l9 was carried for ward to the next year. Though the income was a decrease of £340 on the previous year, the result was marvellous when the many and pressing claims on the generosity of their peoiale were taken into account, such as the 20th Century Fund, the War Funds and the Indian Famine Fund. The amount contributed by the Liverpool district, of which their society was a part, was £6,884. The Warrington circuit contributed £2OO, which he was sorry to say was a decrease on 1898. Towards that £2OO Bewsey-road had contributed £24 15s from the Sunday collections and the missionary meeting' an increase of £9 on the previous year, and E 3 £lO Os ,1 from subscriptions and private collections, making a total of £34 15s 6 (a.pplause ) The report went on to urge the necessity for generous support. Opp)rtunities in all quarters of the globe were unparal- leled. They had only to train and send out men t) carry the message of salvation to the whole of the world. As the dawn of the new century opmed they saw opening out all over the world, in ways they could not conceive of, opportunities for carrying the gospel to willing ears that had never before been permitted to mankind since the days of Christ. Let everyone engaged in the work whether collector or contributor, do their utmost by gifts, work, and prayer to bring about the day when the gospel would be preached to every creature. (Ap- plause.) The CHAIRMAN said he was oaly a stop-gap—(laughter) —but be had consented to be present and preside for three reasons, first, because he could not help it—

(laughter)—secondly, because he bad a great respect for the gentleman who should have presided, and thirdly, tvcausn he was a Christian. He c,-4tal not conce've a man who was a Cnristian and was not in sympathy with the foreign mission cause. Ho was heart and soul in thorough sympathy with the great work being carried out all over the world in the mission field. (applause.) The Rev. W. TOMLINSON, at the outset of his addreF•s, congratulated the Chairman upon the honour that day conferred upon him, and also upon the f4ct that the first public duty he had performed since his electi, n was to preside at a missionary meeting. (Hear, hear.) Pro- ceeding to spe ,k of missionary work in China, Mr Tom- linson said there was no country under Heaven of which, in proportion to its extent, so little was known up to a ;lon time ago, and which had been so MiF- understood and misrepresented as China. It was the custom a few year ago to represent China as a kind of fairy-land, and to throw over everything connected with it a glamour of romance. It required a very brief resi- dence there and a very slight acquaintance with the social condition of the people to disabuse one's mind for ever of all kinds of romance in connection with mission work in China. There were in China nearly four hundred millions of human beings with souls as precious as their own, created by the same Father, and redeerced by the shed- ding of the sune precious blood which ransotned us. div.head: • t 4. I
div.p: A • t 4. I
NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football.

[By " OvaUsti The Warrington team gave the utmost satisfaction to Its admirers on Saturday, when a strong team from Rochdale was defeated at Wilderspool by 21 points to ml. Nobody expected such a result, and least of all, the visitor% There has been nothing in Warrington'a per- formances during the season to warrant;the supposition that Rochdale Hornet?, who had:only lost one match, would wat such a severe troulcing. It seemed quite likely that the Hornets would distinguish themselves in the other direction, and record their first win on the Warrington enclosure. That they hoped to do this was quite evident, in fact a special train brought a number or enthwiasts from the vc.lley of the Roach who expectr d nothing else.

Prior to the match I had a short conversation with one of the officials of the Rochdale Club, and he had an air of quiet confidence about him which appeared to bode ill for Warrington. The Hornets had done so well and the people liked the new ground so much, that the club had taken on no less than 500 new members this season, and the gates had increased by 50 per cent. This is excellent tribute to the truth of the saying thathnoth- ing succeeds like success," and it must be deemed dis- tinctly unfortunate from a Rochdale point of view that the tide of success turned so suddenly and overwhelm- ingly on Saturday.

In this column last week I predicted some good foot- ball if not an actual win for Warrington in the Rochdale match. And good football there was in plenty, though it was rather one-sided. The game was exceedingly fast and open, the bracing day appearing to suit the speedy Warrington men admirably. The Hornets certainly had an "off-day" for their display in the back division was surely too bad to be true after what we have heard during the last few weeks. Warrington's combin- ation was as superior as that of Oldham generally is when they visit Wilderspooi, and the backs ran through and through the Horntts—and without getting stung— re- peatedly.

div.head: To paraphrase some well-known lines •" 0. Rochdale where is thy victory? 0, Hornets where is tLy sting?
div.p: To paraphrase some well-known lines •" 0. Rochdale where is thy victory? 0, Hornets where is tLy sting?

From first to last there was only one team in It and few first-class teams have been so seldom dangerous as were the Hornets on Saturday. Right from the kick-off Warrington took up the offensive and raids on the Roch- dale line were unceasing. Duckworth was the first man to break through, and his try came as the result of a very clever dribble from the pack.HiCknowledge of the sister code has often cows iu useful. Fish added a goal and before half-time contributed a try and a second goal, so that ten points divided the teams at the interval.

Rochdale kooked like making one great effort on resumption but Warrington were too good in every department and betore Img the tale of woe was taken up again. Isherwood, Burgess. and Fish all crossed the line, and the latter kicked another goal, bringing the total to three goals, five trie. against uil.

Every try was the outcome of excellent combined play and there was not the semblance of a fluke connected with a single point. Ths two half-backs and the two centres were in tip-top form and kept the visitors in fear and trembling all afcernoon, while Fish wai übiquitous. I was glad to see Isherwood so much like his old self, and the opening he made for Fish near the close was one of his best efforts in first-class football. Hockenhall on the right was the only weak spot in the team's attack, and a speedier, stronger man would be an acquisition. Dickenson looks like filling the centre position admirably, and he oould find a crack wing plenty to do. He shaped like an old hand against the Hornets. Our full-back and forwards also deserve high praise, though the latter still lack weight in the "scrum. 'y

Field was the best man on his side, and played a very fine individual game. Ef fi• is wonderfully clever in dodg— ing through the opposing backs, but has a bad fault in passing. He seems to toss the ball across anylsow,, and oftener than not it went forward and spoiled an excel- lent opening. Allen was the best of the half baeks, Berrill being a failure,but it certainly would have needed a good pair to cope with Burgess and Duckworth, who were as quick as lightning at times, awl always worked well together. Their old fault of selfishnfsi seems to have worn off. By the way "Billy Rigg was not as good as usual. He allowed himself to be caught far too often. In the front rank of the visitors there appeared to be shirkers, for there was no lack of either bulk or strength.

Fish was the object of considerable attention, but it was no use, and he credited himself with 12 points be- fore the close. In the last three matches he has scored 31 points—sure:y a record in Northern Union football. He 13 a gem of the first water. Oh for such another r

Warrington have risen a place or two and ought to climb higher if present form is maintained. They possess far and away the best scoring averagq of any club near them, and in fact only Swinton and Oldham p'siess a better record of ppints for aad against. This is a hopsful augury for the future.

Houghton turned out and was a tßwer of strength at full back. He did what ho has done several timi's before,and that was—Eccred a try. Well done" Knox "—still evergreen.

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.
Stockton Heath v. Horwich.

At Stockton Heath on Saturday, the home team quickly forced the game and Gibbon drew first blood within five minutes of the start. The Horwich goal- keeper kept out a sulendid attempt from Dickinson, and the homestrrs were rewarded shortly afterwards,Gandy converting the poss from centre. Horwich now troubled the home defence, hut were quickly repul,ied, and from good fcriward play Gibbon again scored, to be quickly followed by another from D:ckinson, the result of a good shot from a penalty corner. At half time the score was Stockton Reath, four goals; Horwich, none. In the second half the home team scored through Gibbon (two) ard Owen, thus winning by seven goals to none. Thi, visitors' goalkeeper saved well and the left wing were most prominent. The home half backs were a good trio, and of the forwards tbe home captain worked ad- mirably in the centre.
