Irregular atteniance cantinues to be the torment of many B )ard Schools throughout the country,and where it is a torn sat there is hope For there are elucat.onal authorities that can SOTH)O77 reg..rd irregularity of attendance with the utmost uncoa. cern, and in these cases the faul,-, has to be divided between the parents and the local authority. Some of the smaller School Boards, especially, display little anxiety to enforce the law. If parents are ind,fferent and school attendance officers not over- zealous, the Boards which take the view that educa- tion is not of much value, are not likely to b 3 very severe either on officers or p treats. Unfortunately it has to be said that although a generation has grown up since the law made attendance at school at least nominally compulsory, there are large num- bers of people who fail to appreciate the advantages of education for their children. A sense of respon- sibility might be qaickened in their case by the imposition of the more substantial fines allowed under the new Act. llagistrates could certainly help to retorm the really ba I cases by dealing severely with those who repeatedly come before them.

div.head: EXA M[N EU.
div.p: THE EXA M[N EU.
NOVEMBER 16111 1900.
THE history of the aCabinets, Large Cabinet is one of evolu- and Small.

tion. It is no recognised part of the British Constitution. Formerly, a Committee of the Privy Council sat, under the presidency of the Sovereign, for the transaction of Government business. A time came when the Sovereign could not speak English, and then the Committee deliberated apart. The result is the present Cabinet. It has always included the four Secretaries of State, the First Lord of the Treas- ury, the Chancellor of the Exchequor, and the Lord Chancellor and the Lord President, with the Secretary for War and the First Lord of the Admiralty. Ten Ministers would seem to be the irreducible minimum. When the number rose to thirteen and fifteen the Cabinet seemed to be a large one. In the last Government, just re- constructed into fragments, there were eighteen Ministers, because persons like the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, the Lord Chancellor of Ireland, the Lord-Lieutenant, and the Post- master-General were included. The newly-consti- tuted Ministry seams likely to be the largest we have ever had, and to consist of twenty members. Such a Cabinet is far too large for ordinary busi- ness and for general deliberations. It will follow that there roust be sub-division. There will be a small group of there orfour persons who will settle all delicate questions, and act as the inner Cabi- net under the direction of the Prime Minister, and their colleagues will have nothing else to do but obey this junta. It has been found convenient to act in this way ever since Lord SALISBURY resumed power in 1895, and some contradictions are accounted for by divisions of Ministers, with secret instructions by one or two members. A large Cabinet offers advantages in the way of deal- ing with legislative projects. They can be debated generally in the whole Cabinet, remitted to Sub- Committees, and then re-examined as a whole after the drafting has taken place. Fewer councils are thus required in dealing with a large amount of work, and several measures may be cleverly handled in detail whilst the more serious linos of policy are under the consideration of the chiefs of the party. But the cynic may ask, if a Cabinet of twenty be found better than one of thirteen or fifteen, why should the number be re- stricted to twenty ? Several officials might be in- cluded now outside, and with inferior rank. The law advisers of the Government, the Senior Whip, and one or two others are capable men whose opinions are worth having. Cabinet rank might. however, become too cheap, and that is the obvious tendency of large Cabinets. When we come to close quarters, we may ask what is the value upon foreign or colonial affairs, upon India or the army and the navy, of the views of the CHANCELLOR of the Duchy of Lancaster, the POSTMASTER- GENERAL, or the President of the Board of Agri- culture? What can the Lord CHANCELLOR of Ire- land know about a social question in England ? And what can be the importance to the Cabinet on a question of finance of the views of the First Commissioner of Works? Probably Lord SALIS- BURY has been balancing parties. He has added one Liberal Unionist and he has added one Con- servative. With fifteen Conservatives and five Liberal Unionists it can hardly be said that the latter have too much power, and if Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN can dominate a Cabinet of eighteen he may be unable to overbear a Cabinet of twenty. These considerations may have influenced the PRIME MINISTER, who is known to be somewhat cynical in such matters, and he may think that he has reduced the height of any one man besides him- self by adding more men to obscure it. In other words, he has increased his own personal weight by adding to the number of Ministers who will obediently follow him in everything. It is a pretty game, bat it cannot be concealed from the antagonist against whom it is directed, and pro- bably the result may be of a character wholly un- reopen.

FINANCIAL men do not Are our Financial like the outlook. They illusions Ending ? say that it would be more profitable to add something permanently to the National Debt, to raise it small Transvaal Loan, and to remit some taxation. But this would be very easy finance, and we have had sadly too much of it of late years. Sir M. IlicKs-BEAcH does not intend, he plainly says, to leave the cost of the war as an addition to the permanent burden of the country. We think he is right in principle and in justice. Our debt is still large, and it represents wars waged in the past when our revenue resources were not as good as they are now. The country has determined on systemati- eally reducing the permanent debt, and some part of the reduction ordered has been already arrested, to prevent undue taxation. We could not in- crease the debt itself without the most urgent necessity, for a diminishing debt means increasing credit, and an increasing debt the reverse. The arrangement for gradually pay- ing off the money we have borrowed for the , war is one of the secrets to be kept until March. War is always more attractive whoa I somebody else is going to pay the bill, and when we entered upon a war withthe Boer States Ice confidently expected that one of them would be rich enough to pay the biggest part of the account. That belief has been gradually losing a part of its fascination. The minerals of the Transvaal will have to bear some part of the burden, and happilY the mines are intact. LORD ROBERTS was so anxious to secure Johannesburg and the Rand that he made a dash across the Vaal, and left many things to be done afterwards which he would otherwise have done before he left Bloemfontein. If the war is the longer for his strategy, we have saved a part of the wealth which will assist in liquidating the war debt. The mine owners are saying beforehand that they cannot stand heavy taxation, and:that they are poorer than we imagine. These are clever pleas, and yet they cannot be , allowed to prevail. Some substantial contributions will have to be made. On the other hand, instead of two rich colonies being annexed, we shall find ourselves with two countries despoiled by war and raids, with many Boers already migrated to ,Damaraland, and with no sources ,of wealth except in minerals. The annexed colonies will not pay the whole cost of the war' The CHANCELLOR of the Exchequer is candid when he remarks" there must necessarily be a large part of the cost which will have to be met by the tas- payers of this country." Surely there are illusions the other way? If so, they are ending, and we can see why the country was asked for a political verdict before it had got the war bill. There will be no reduction of taxation next year. There ma)! even have to be an increase of taxation. The first is certain ; the second is almost equally so. Not only to meet the war, but:to meet other sequen- tial expenses, the Income-tax will probably go UP 2d or 4d in the 2. Some indirect taxes must also

be increased or new ones .invented, in order to equalise matters. Another group of pleasant illusions will vanish. The revenue may keep up, but trade is not as good as it was, and high taxa- tion injures business and checks 'speculation. The financial outlook is thus far from being touched with roseate hues. We shall have to pay for glory, and even our patriotism will mean expenditure. Conservative rule is always costly. There are persons who have denied the assertion. They are now beginning to understand its old and now significance.

IT is pleasant to not o that the American Press at least generally sympathises with the views .on the conditions of the America Cup contest which have been expressed in this country, while som e papers are strong supporters of change. It is fel that to revive the interest of the public in yacht- ing, and help to give the country a host of seamen in time of need, racing should take place on ocean course, if not actually across the ocean. en Each contestant it is argued should have a perfectly free run, with plenty of sea room: and an opportunity to prove her seaworthiness in all weathers, and with no chance to win or lose by blanketing or crossing the course of another. The race of 1901, it is recognised' candidly, is likely to be the last of its kind. The challenger, it is admitted, is tremendously handi- capped, for she has to be built at least strop g enough to get somehow across the Atlantic, whereas the (o.efender need only be planned to meet the smooth seas which prevail about SandY Hook under the influence of those calms which had such disastrous effect upon the racing on the last occasion. And when the races are over both vessels are absolutely useless. There is a waste of money and, what is still worse, a waste of energy in yacht designing and building which is depler- able. There is thus a confident expectation 03 both sides of the Atlantic that after next year the conditions of this particular contest will be so fer altered as to make it a trial of science and skill directed towards some really useful end.

How many people will this year watch through the silent hours of the night in the hope that their vigil may be rewarded by the spectacle of a glorious display of Leonids ? Last year at about this time they were confidently expected, but tha hope was doomed to disappointment. This year, if they make their appearance at all they shoula have the cordial welcome which is given to friend? who were known to be close at hand, but on bus" ness which was believed practically certain to carrY them past our doors. Yet it must be admitted that in bringing about this belief conjecture plaYs at least as great a part as calculation. It is knol that the earth will pass into the region where, the great meteor stream continued to flow as 1" has done during the first three quarters of the cell' tury, a magnificent shower of Loonids would, b: inevitable. But there is reason to belles; specially after the failure of la st year, that 5110 perturbations of the streamhavo taken place as divert its orbit by three millions of miles, 0b trifling matter astronomically speaking, andlhis sufficient to prevent our atmosphere catching iY or next year in its net more than one or two sv)-`4, specimens of these wanderers of space, which, the great years of the past, have been eneouritert; in shoals. For the present these meteors must "iv reckoned, as a" Times:' correspondent haPPitio puts it, as the lost Leonids. Yet they are riot be regarded as permanently departed. If by, t';' means their orbit and number conld he defluitablYe ascertained further perturbations could als° foreseen, and astronomers would be able t s-r's precisely when the great periodic meteor of the Leonids will present themselves agairi, the delight of our posterity.

He has well merited this retit?sva of confidence for thronghout a year full of strio.lls responsibilities be upheld the dignity of his °fli„i''! and of the town in a manner which gave unclu-ild fled satisfaction to everybody. The Council cou do nothing less, last week, than unaniraously heartily re-elect Alderman Roberts, audit wba: pleasant to see such good feeling and Bens? of t fitness of things everywhere displayed. Time vi 7.2:, when the election of a Liberal Nonconforrn 1,b5 Mayor in Warrington would have been impussi.bdlee..' and the very suggestion a sonrce uf v" spread disaffection and ill-feeling. t whatever his political and religious beliefs may be. These are the days of wider toleration, and the Warrington Town Council has shown itself as capable of fair and generous treatment as any Public body in the country. The Mayor has been re-elected solely on his merits —which are nunterous—and we do not think the Council was ever better pleased with its own selec- tion. In a sense too they re-elected the Mayoress, who has captivated the Council and the townspeople by her personal charm and evident earnest desire to assist her husband to the fullest Possible extent. She is hardly the "dark hors" Alderman Francomb styled her in his enigmatical compliment, but rather the fair lady who has won all hearts.

The average ratepayer has only a hazy notion of 'what the Corporation accomplishes during a Municipal year. He is impressed principally with the fact that a lot of money is being spent and that certain improvements—such as Bridge-street—the need of which is daily brought under his notice, trogress but slowly. Consequently ho grumbles. F+evg the average ratepayer is in a majority, and it Is necessary therefore that these erroneous Ideas of his should be combated with Incontrovertible and reassuring facts. Such a task was that of the Mayor, after he bad returned thanks for re-election. We recommend every ratepayer to study carefully, and with open blind, the eloquent, concise statement of town's affairs which the Mayor •delivered. From it he NMI so that not only has much money been spent but a great deal has been accomplished with it and while he will note that proposals for spending Ear, ther huge sums are mentioned, he cannot over-6 leek the pleasing fact that the rateable value of the town has rapidly increased and now stands at .the big figure of £254,000, while other sources of future inccme and the lightening of taxation will Presently be available. We are indeed "citizens of no mean city," and when the schemes for elec- tric light, tramways, new police buildings, tech- nical schools, street improvements, and open air BP.aees are complete and out of hand, Warrington will be a town on a par with the rapid advance of ivilization and science instead of lagging 50 years behind, as the stock reproach has it.

sow that the elections, Parliamentary and Muni- Cipal, are over, this appears to be regarded as a h.ttintz opportunity for the great enfranchised to Rive those whom it may concern a little of their Mind about canvassing and canvassers. The number Of those who inwardly object to house-to-house soliciting of votes is probably legion. The practice Is, undoubtedly, one that leads to mach mischief, to lying hypocrisy, and deceit as between man and Man. Besides which, a straightforward and really "free and independent elector" does not care for, and is often annoyed by the sudden and extravagant interest in his personal and family welfare ,developed by the canvasser at election times Mach might be done toward the suppression of the evil by th-i candidates themselves calling meetings of the electorate arid addressing them en mane. Such meetings Would afford ample opportunity for them to explain their views and intentions to the constituency, and for the free ventilation of matters of general interest and importance. This method has been adopted in some towns with the very best results, and might with advantage be extended to many others. It is fairly well under- stood, ae between canvas-etc and canvas* d, th it promises made in individual cases, are of the pro- wrbial pie-crust order. In the majority of in- stances, they are as readily forgotten as they were made. The Ballot Act wai for awhile one of the Lebt, abused pieces of modern legislation, but when people began to generally recognise the fairness sad 3ustice of its principles, there came with that re- ceznition also a desire to give the Act fair play. But this has not been dons, nor can it ever be so 12,_nR as canvassing and the conveyance of voters to poll continues to be legalised and practised. Both practices are not only evils in themselves, but 1.1..rl in direct contravention of the spirit and inten- tion of the legislature.

div.head: FIRE ON THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: FIRE ON THE SHIP CANAL.

On the Ship Canal,at Frodsham Marsh, near Run- corn, on Friday night, about eleven o'clock, a watchman discovered that a jetty formerly used for tipping dredgings from the canal on to the marsh, but which was idle, was on fire. fie imme- diately telephoned to Runcorn, but the flames had obtained such a hold that the jetty was practically destroyed before aid could be rendered, the jetty being in a very isolated position. The captain of the dredger Salford, en raute for Manchester, saw the fire, and had the hole put in readiness for use, but the fierceness of the flames prevented him tak• ing his craft sufficiently near for the hose to be effective, A. large 60-ton crane craihed through the stage into the water, considerably narrowing the navigable portion of the waterway, but a portable pumping-engine fortunately remained on the em- bankment. the fire exhausted itself in the early hours of Saturday morning. The damage is roughly net down at between £2,000 and £3,000. How the fire originated is unknown. WESToN WESLIMLN CHURCH.

The old school in which the Wesleyans of Weston Point taught their young ones was opened in 1872, but owing to the growth of the village in recent years, the members have been compelled to provide a much more commodious and up-to-late building, which was finished and out of the hands of the contractor, Mr J Sefton, of Runcorn, a few weeks ago. On Wednesday afternoon last a large con- gregation assembled there, and after the singing of a hymn, Mr Boston, of Frodsbam, formally ppened the schoolroom. Upon assembling inside the Rev A Wells (superintendent minister) conducted the service,and the Rev J A B Malvern preached an elo- quent sermon.Subsequenuly Mrs F J Norman, Run( o unfurled a beautiful new banner. In the evening after a public tea there was a great meeting pre- sided over by Mr T Simister, Runcorn, at which addresses were delivered by the circuit ministers, Rev J A B Malvern, and Messrs A R Norman and R H Posnett.

A meeting of the order was field on Saturday, in the Greenwa3-road School, under the presidency of Mr Thomas R ‘Vhyte. There was a fair attendance of mambers. A fraternal visit was paid by two members from the Weston division, viz, Messrs John Brown and William Ilazlehurst, the former giving an address, The financial secretary, Mr James Johnson, in a statement with regard to the position of the order, said they had over £5OO in the central fund. This was satisfactory, c.)nsidering the short time the fund had been formed. A nuoa- bar of officers then gave short addressel, inducing Messrs Alfred Noden, Thomas J Holt, D Bishrown, Thomas Heesom, Thomas Clarke, and Samuel Tom- linson. Mr E 'ward Key, senr, gave an interesting address, in which he emphasised the importance of training the young to avoid and set their faces azainst intoxicating drink, lie warmly commended the lecture which had been given in the day schools in Runcorn and district on the aciontific aspect of the temperance question.

NIGHT POA.CITrNG ON NORTON PRTOR.Y ESTATF: At the Runeorn Police Court, on Friday, before F J Norman (in the chair) and Mr W Handley. William John Talbot, and John Wilkinson, both of Weston Point. were charged on remand with night poaching on land in the oceupation of Sir R Brooke, Bart, at Halton, on the sth inst., and fur- ther with assaulting Joseph lior;on,a keeper at the same time and place. The prisoners pleaded guilty to poaching, and Wilkinson admitted that it was he who committed the assault.—From the evidence of George Rigby, head gamekeeper to Sir R M. Brooke, it appeared that he went id company with two other keepers, to the Old Pits Cover, just below Halton Cemetery, at six o'clock on Nlonday evening, They had been there about 40 minutes when he saw the two men come along the wood side. Witness and the other keepers gave chase, and prisoners got over a gate. They tirsn commenced stoning witness and his assistants, and one of the stones struck Horton. A keeper named West se- cured Wilkinson. and witness went after Talbot. ' After going some ten or a dozen yards Talbot told witness to stand back, and commenced to search his pockets Witness found the prisoner in possossion of a loaded gun. The weapon was in two pieces, and prisoner had the stock in one pocket and the barrel in the other. He was also in possession of the shot-bag and powder-fltsk produced. Witness had heard firing going on at, the Old Pits Cover several nights previously, and that was the reason why he went there on Monday night. He took the Iprisoners to Halton and handed them over to P.C. Upton. He had known Wilkinson a long time, but he only knew Talbot by sight. He took proceedings against Wilkinson 20 years ago. —By Mr Handley: The men were on Sir Richard Brooke's estate, and they were in the cover when they commenced to run,—Juseph Horton, assistant keeper, in the em- ploy of Sir Richard Brooke, corroborated.—Albert West, assistant keeper, also gave evidence. Wilkin- son made an attempt to run away, but stumbled, and witness struck him one blow as he was falling. He had previously told Wilkinson to stop throwing —The prisoner Talbot said either Horton or West told Wilkinson he had a good mind to knock his brains out. He (prisoner) admitted they were out for the purpose of oaching.—Wilkinson said he threw the stone.—Prisoners wore etch fined 20 and 8s 61 costs for the poaching, or 14 days' hard labour, and Wilkinson was tined 20i and 6s costs for the assault, or 14 day' hard labour. They were in addition, bound over in the sum of £lO each with a security of L 5 each to be of good behaviour for the next twelve months.

that they should go into the matter minutely. The Coairman slid the question had ben asked: Why h 3.0 not the County Councils taken shares in the under- taking ? He (the Chairman) k lew that in 1814 the then authorities said they were satisfied with the road through Warrington as being the most direct road through the two couotiea. That was a position they bad stuck to up to the present day. The solicitors to the pro- meters tdd them at the interview that they never expsc- td the County Councils to take any money in it; so they were not disappointed. Someone wilted what benefit the scheme would be to the workingmen. Surely it would be an advantage to have another way of getting over to Widues without mounting those steps to the foot-bridge. He was surprised at the remarks made about the Possibility of carrying brine across the bridge. The following section of the Act prohibited such a thing being done :—" The company shall not without express Parliamentary powers convey, or authorize or permit to be conveyed, any brine in any pipe, trough, or sough, or the like in, upon, over, or under the bridge by this Act authorised," (Applause.) The present debt of Runcorn was something like £12,000. That was exclusive of the waterworks debt, which was in the nature of a trade deb, and private street works. The latter was a debt which came back to them ; it was simply borrowed for toe time being. As far as toe waterworks was con- c irned. except for two years, when they had taken a penny in the £ from the rates owing to the rise in coal, toe undertaking had paid its way, and it was evident to all that it had been a great public convenience. With regard to the hours the bridge would be open he (the Chairman) knew that it was stated last January in their interview that it would be open from five o'clock in the morning until eleven at night, and. if the traffic demanded it, it would be opened longer, open all night. The Conceit had not lost sight of this matter. Toe hope was held out that an arrangement would be come to with the London and North-Western Railway Company whereby contractors' tickets over the trane- porter would be available for the footbridge. Whether that would tos provided for they did not know. (Laugh- ter). They gave it to them f r what it was worth. But the footbridge would still be in rxistenm Mr. Boden said he would like to koow whether any of the Urban District Council bad taken any shares in this bridge?

The Chairman said none of the urban councillors had taken shares in the bridge, for the reason that no shares had yet been placed in the market. Mr Boden.—ls it not a fact that one member only of the Urban Council will take shares in this bridge? Mr S Taylor—Name the gentleman. Mr Boden—Mr Posnett. Mr Taylor asked who had given him such informa tion ? Mr Hewitt—l said so.

Mr Taylor—How do you know what councillors will- do? We have had no opportunity. They are not put be fore the public. Mr J J Bowyer proposed the following resolution:— "This meeting or the inhabitants of Runcorn, convened by public advertisement in the three local newspapers, expresses its opinion that it is advisable for the Urb in District Council, on behalf of the township of Runcorn, to invest in the shares of the Widnes and Runcorn Bridge Uodertaking such a sum, not exceeding £lO,OOO, as will entitle to representation on the directorate, such sum to be invested in accordance with, and subject to the provisions of the Widnes and Runcorn Briige Act 1900." Mr Morris seconded. Mr 11 H Possett supported the idea of having represen- tation on the Board of Directors.
Mr S Taylor strongly supported the scheme, and said he should vote for the town having an interest in the scheme.

Me Imison said he wished to explain that Mr Handley had answered the various questions which had been put from his own point of view. (Hear, bear.) He was in no sense the mouthpiece of the Council, because, as they saw, he did not consult the members. He had no opportunity for doing so, and he (Mr Imison) did not blame him for it. Consequently:they must regard bis remarks as an expression of his (the Chairman's) own individual opinion, and not as in any sense binding on the Council. He certainly was not in favour of putting anything like £lO,OOO in this scheme. He thought they had looming before them some very heavy liabilities that did not justify them in placing additional burdens upon the ratepayers at the present time. He believed in havinz some interest in the scheme, because he thought they would be in a better position to ask the promoters for cmacessione. Mr Henry Dodd moved an amendment to the effect that the resolution authorizing the investment of £5,000 be adherel to. Mr Baden scc)nJed. On a vote being taken 13 only voted\ for the amend- ment, and it was lost.
The orizinal motion by Mr Bowyer was put, ani carriod by a larize majority. A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meet. jag to a close.

div.head: EXADVIINER, FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 16, 1900
div.p: THE EXADVIINER, FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 16, 1900
FARM FIRE AT ASTON.

Between 5 and 5.30 on Sunlay morning, a corn stack on Park Side Farm, Aston-by-Sutton, in the occupation of Mr. RObe,rt Shepherd, was discovered to be on fire by William Worrall, the horseman. The Runcorn Fir,-3 Brigade was summoned with all possible haste, anti they arrived on the scene in g )od time, only to find that their efforts to save the property Were powerless. AU that they could do w,:s to keep the fi tales under control, and prevent them from doing any serious damage to the farm buildings and aijoining property. The whole of the produce was either destroyed or rendered unfit for use, and when it is stated that the farm is one of the largest in the neighbourhood, sir. Shepherd having something like 100 head of milking stock, it will be understood what destruction the fire wrought. The Fire Brigade was engaged on the burning and smouldering mass almost the whole of Sunday. The damage is estimaten at £1,500 The produce is fully covered by insurance. The cause of the conflagration has not yet risen ascertained.— The Runcorn Fire Brigade did not return home until noon on Monday. They wire under the C3M- mand of Superintendent R ibert Wright and Deputy- Superintendent Cousins. In one lln;ch bay alone the pro Ince of 8) arras wit: stored, and t'lis was only a p-irjoi of the stuff dAAroyal. rtp, War- rington Brigade was summoned, but they were met by a mes.enger on horeback, ani told that their services were not required.

div.head: RECKLESS RUNCORN BOATMA.N.
div.p: A RECKLESS RUNCORN BOATMA.N.

At the Wigan B nouga Police C3art on Tnursd ty Samuel Jones, boat captain, 44, C)tion-street, Run- corn, was charged with wilfully damaging a lock gate. the prop3rty of the 143 eds and Liverpool Canal tdompany, on the 19th October.—Mr J Wilson prose- cuted on behalf of the compaoy, and said that the defendant had run his boat into the lock-gates, and after committing the offence he went to Mr Moss, inspector of the company, and said he was willing to pay the damage, as he was anxious that the ma-- ter should not go into court, because he had done the very same thing before and had been fined £5. Mr. Wilson said he was instructed und3r tie cir- cumstances to press for the full penalty, £s.—Wil- liam Clayton, foreman carpenter of the Canal Com- pany, stated that on the 19th ult. he was standing near No. 21 lock, and the defendant came up with two boats, the Lark and th 3 Linnet,. Defendant , was in the steerage of the fi.cat boit (tad his mate was on the towing path. Witnes shouted to de- fendant's mate that the boat must be "strapped" to prevent it running into the gates, and the captain shouted out: "Never mind the gates; I can pay for them." The consequence was that the first boat ran into the lock and strained the gate, beside doing other damage. If the defendant had done as he had been directed, nothing would have happened.— Mr Moss stated that the defendant had offered him £5 to make good the damage.—Defendant was fined £1 and costs and ordered to pay for the damage. BEGGA.ILS TRIPPED AT WIDNES —CLAIMING RELLTIONSIIIP WITH A MAGISTRATE.

Before the Mayor, at the Widne Police 03urt on Monday morning, two old men named James Bios- sington, and John Sadler, were charged wit n beg - ing on Sunday. Ellen Crabtree, a servant in the employ of Alderman sadler, said the two men came to Alderman Sadler's house and asked for alms. The prisoner Sadler asked if Mr. Sadler was at home. She said he was, whereupon he stated that he was a relative, and wished to see him Alderman Sadler was informed, and the prisoner was ushered into the dining-room in the presenc i of the family. —Alderman Sadler stepped into the witness box, and stated that at ten o'clock on Sunday nignt the prisoner came to his house in a drunken state. Before him and his family he told a wandering tale. He had just arrived from South America in search of relatives, and was in want of assistance. tie had also lost his "darling wife and four lovely daughters." Upon being asked if he knew he was talking to a magistrate, he expressed a wish to go at once.—Police-constable Hall deposAd to appre- hending the two men at the instance of the domes- tic servant. He had met both men before in the early part of the evening,and had directed them to Cain's lodging house.—Both men pleaded guilty,and the Mayor in sending them both to gaol for fourteen days, said he was sorry he could not double it MR. A. MOND AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

Mr. S. Taylor presidedever the large audience assembled at the Runcorn Liberal Club, on Tuesday evening, Mr. A. Mond, of Northwich, was the lec- turer, and his subject was" the lesson to be learnt from the last General Election." He illustrated, how, in the past. Liberals always fought for reform on sound principles, as instance the "Corn Laws Repeal "and the" Franchise." They had one issue and one issue only before the country, and fought for it year in year out. Since, however, the Liberal Party had gone in for long programmes, like the Newcastle P ogramme, too much room was allowed for what he might call" faddists.' He urged that the Land Reform question should be the next "battle cry of the Liberals." The last election was peculiar in regard to the fact that whereas it should I have been :the Government who should have been criticised upon their work of the preceding five years, it was the Liberal Party who were criticised. He attributed, in a great measure, the want of unanimity on the part of the Liberal Leaders as being the cause for the lack of adhesion amongst the rank and file of the party. He was in favour of Lord Rosebery being the Liberal Leader, and pointed out that the lesson to be learned was to go back to the principal of fighting for one reform at a time; and that with a view of carrying out those reforms they should educate and organise the party which was still a powerful one. Mr Mond also in the course of his remarks paid a high tribute to the late Mr. Gladstone.—An animated discussion fol- lowed, after which Mr W Handley proposed and Mr T Dean seconded a vote of thanks to the lec- turer, which was heartily accorded.

div.head: RUNOORN TRANSPORTER BRIDGE. Meeting of Ratepayers. £lO,OOO to be Invested.
div.p: RUNOORN TRANSPORTER BRIDGE. Meeting of Ratepayers. £lO,OOO to be Invested.

On Monday evening a public meeting of rate- payers was held in the *Drill Hall, Runcorn, for the pur- pose of conftrring with the Urban District Council as to the amount oh money the GNU:MiI should invest in shares in the Widnee and Runcorn Transporter Bridge, to be constructed under the Widnes and Ruecorn Bridge Act, 1930.-51 r W Haudley, chairman of the C,uncil, pre- sided, and there were also present the following ,aem- hers of the Council—Messrs B J Grice, D Bisbrce- H Salkeld, J W Lightburn, E 'nelson, R Ii Posnett. J Wil- seri, James Pritchard. S Taylor. MJ S weetmin, Dean, S Walton, E Gatley, F A Lake (aw clerk to the Olt:v- -eil), and E Marshall (secretary and accountant). There was only a moderate attendance. The Chairman said that that meeting was rather a new departure on the part of the Urban District Council, but as this was an important question affecting the future wall-being of Runcorn there were some members of the Council who thought that it was only fair that they should confer with the inhabitants before tak- ing definite action. Alluding to the Bill he said she -tly that the clauses that they got were obtaisecl for Runcorn'alprotection, that their concerns should not be unduly interfered !with, and that they miebt be put in as good a position as they were to-day. That with re- spect to the fares over the bridge the charge should not be more than a penny each way, and that with regard to weekly contracts they should not be more than the present charge across the bridge, viz, one shilling per week. These terms were insisted on, and they sue ceeded in getting them. They gave them (the Council) other concessions, viz : Family tickets and pass tickets for firms, and all those were embodied in the Bill that received the Royal assent. The Manchester Snip Canal Company succeeded iu getting a clause that , there should be a wharf placed at the bottom of Watei- ' Joe-road, at the end of Church-street, thus opening up the Ship Canal for local traffic, and in a way laying its ' banks open to the world, re that wharf was to be u•esd for the transhipment of goed9 Chet might be sent any- where. The next step was embodied in a letter received, from the solicitors, dated July 24de 1900. Too encl(..l sures were also included in that communication. The letter referred to a clause or clauses under the Act,which provided that the Urban Council of Runcorn and the Corporation of Widnes, and the County Councils of Lan- cashire and Cheshire, if they thought fit, to subscribe an amoult. could take an interest in the erection and subsequent uss of the bridge as intended to be built. The letter was remitted to a committee to ceniider Bat the Council met on October 18',:h and had a long Ms.. cussion but ultimately they adjourned the meeting from the morning to the evening, and in the meantime a deputation went down to have an interview with the solicitors. They beard that Widnes had decided a few days before to put in the scheme the large amount of £25,000 and that seemed to tie their hands in the SAiss that they would have to follow suit, not to that extent but to a somewhat proportionate amount. kt the ad- journed meeting the Council pas.ed a resolution resolv- ing that £5,000 be invested in shares in the said company on the condition that the Lo- cal G wernment Board sanctioned the matter. Teat resolution • was sent ito the solicitors, and a reply was received whiclistated, in effect, that while they would be very pleased to accept the £5,000 shares, they did not consider it was sufficient to entitle Runcorn to oppoint a Director. If they subscribed £lO,OOO they would have the right to nominate one director. It was only right that he (the chairman) should put before them what an investment of £lO,OOO in this scheme would involve, so that they might consider it in all its bearines. The urban district assessable value was £47.000, which, at a penny in the pound would yield £195. The actual yield last year was however, only £lB4, and thsrefore, they based it on that calculation. Now, to borrow a sum of £lO,OOO for a period of 30 years at 3i per cent.—which was the highest sum they had paid tor some little time involved £526 15/ 53 a year. That in 30 years would pay off prineipal and interest, and they would have £lO,OOO at the end of that time in hand as a capital sum. This would mean a charge on the rates of a fraction under 3 1 in the £. Supposing they took it at3l in the £, under the Act there was a provision for paying interest as shares during the period of contraction named in the Act—that .was seven years—but it was limited by a proviso that not more than £5.000 should be so paid away in interest. The bridge was estimated to be finished and in working order in two years from the time that it was commenced. They would receive this 3 per cent., as fixed by the Act, durinif the period of construction. This would amount to £3OO per year that they would receive. That wouldl lower the £526 15s 5d to an annual payment of £226 153 sd, which would be chargeable on the rates. That would mean a fraction under lid in the 2. After it was constructed they would be dependent on the re venue that the bridge created. In the letter it infers that it would be a paying concern. It might be so, and it might not. They bad better look at it from every point of view. Many members believed it would be a paying concern. If it paid 3 per cent. only, the annual charge of thirty years on the present ratable value would be £226 155 5d ; if it paid 4 per cent., the amount would be £126 15s sd, or just over if is the 2. If it paid 5 Per cent'. it would be lowered to £26 15s sd, or equal to id in the £. If it paid beyond 5 per cent. there would Pe a profit in reduction of their rates. He believed there were also two other estimates He referred to two communications that had come to hand, one being a statement from the directors themselves as to the bridge, and the other a report on the probable traffic. This report was the report of Mr. S B Cotrell, general manager of the Liverpool Overhead Railway. The gist of it was—and Mr. Cottrell's estimates were based on a very wide experience—that the revenue from the trans porter bridge would be £12,000 per year. It seemed rather a big estimate to the Council. They could not exactly get to know what was the revenue of the pre- sent footbridge, but the footbridge was restricted to passenger traffic only. This £12,000 took in an estimated revenue, from goods as well as passeneer traffic hut if this was reduced by a quarter it would leave £9,000 of a revenue. Then he estimated that it would take something like £l,OOO to pay working expenses, and if they doubled that, and said £2,000, there would still be £7,000 left of this reduced estimate with which to meet the interest on the shares. That meant something like six per cent.—a fraction under six per cent, on the esti- mated expenditure of £120,000, which was the estimated expenditure for the erection of the bridge, and putting it in working order. Questions being invited, Mr. Gittens inquired what benefit the bridge was go- ing to be to the working men if the charge Was going to be not less than is per week. Mr. Chadwich said it seemed to him to be perfectly

div.head: RUNCORN NOTESi
div.p: RUNCORN NOTESi

[By a Correspondent]. The meeting of ratepayers at Runcorn with regard to the investment of .£lO,OOO iu the proposed Transporter Bridge gives us much food for reflec- tion. The question asked by Mr. Meadowcroft, considering his official position, as to the ratable value of Runcorn compared with ten years ago seemed very unfortunate. A. little reflection suggests that ten years ago was just before the opening and completion of the Ship Canal. If a working man by dint of hard saving and struggling self-denial built a cottage in which to end his days so as to save him resorting to the commin- igie palatial residence at Dutton, the ratable value of Runcorn is increased by at least five per cent on the cost of his cottage, but it would seem, from the answer given to Mr. Meadowcroft's question that the ratable value of Runcorn is practically the same as it was ten years ago, that the millions spent at and near Runcorn by the Mancheiter Ship Canal Company have not benefited its ratable value to any appreciable extent, tut rather points to the conclusion that the ratable value of the Company's property in Runcorn may be less now than it was then.

During the last few weeks I have heard frequent reference to the abortive vehicular bridge of which Ir Wiswall is cre lited with largely being sponsor. No doubt such a bridge would have been an excel- lent if not an ideal means of communication between the two sides of the river, but viewed from its' financial aspect" it might have proved disastrous to the ratepayers of Runcorn. I under- stand it has been stated by Mr Wiswall that the " Vehicular " would have been a free bridge. If this be correct and no';a lapsus lingua how cam.° it about that the late Board of C3namissioners of which I be! eve Mr Wiswall was at the time chairman and Mr 11 adowcroft one of its members passed a reso- lution pledging ibe ratepayers to a contribution ofi £30,000, a 8110 a which would have meant an sauna payment of .C 1,600 or an addition to the rates or over:eight-pence in the .C; and this without possi' bility of any direct revenue. This too with it horizon darkening with the cloud of unparalleled depression following 1891, often described as Run- cgrn's "darkest hour," when it was depicted in our Council Chamber as litt!e more than a deserted village with its works at a standstill, many of its shops struggling on, or with closed shutters, 700 of its cottriges tenantleiss, and Dr McDougall wisely pointing out that every inducement should be held out by low rating to attract new industries to Runcorn and that no expenditure should be in curred which would in any way add to the gloomy outlook. If judging from the unanimity with which such a resolution was 'passed Runcorn could then with a light heart and without the support of a public meeting afford an addi- tional burden of £30,000 and with no prospect of a reNulting revenue, how is it that Runcorn with its brighter outlook and increasing trade cannot now afford to invest in the Transporter Bridge one third of the amount with a certainty of a large indirect benefit in the reduction of the fare for crossing and a probable, may I not safely say, certain revenue from the increased facilities such a structure will afford not only to Runcorn and Widnes but the large surrounding district ?

Another matter which is putting itself to the front is the political activity of our friends the Tories. Indeed, they seem so enamoured of their positinn that they have pushed out a challenge, and on this point Mr Samuel Taylor, at the Liberal Club on Tuesday night expressed himself fearlessly, lie said he was prepared for one to take up the chal- lenge and have " local " questions fought out on political lines. This is acceptable to the majority of the Liberal Party, and is in fact what they have been asking for for a considerable time. Mr Taylor as he himself admitted, has been a decided draw- back to the cause, in this one reApect, for hitherto he has always fought local i.ff•tirs on what he is pleased to call a broader issue. Now, r,ow3ver, the road is cleared, and we are told the Liberal Party are prepared to exert t liemselves,and fight for their principles as they ought to have done many years ago.

When I ventured to discuss some months ago the efficiency of the road making of Runcorn, it reached my ears that offence was being given in certain quarters,and as I did not like giving offence,especi- ally when it was apparent that the responsible Forties were doing their best I desisted, Now, it is my duty to remind the public of what I predicted, and show the fruits of the work to the light of day. L

Will anyone t3ll me how much the crossing from Doctor's Bridge to the Cleveland Hotel has been im- proved, or indeed any other street in the town ; and if any street, are improved to a decided extent,will that person also tell me if the improvement is in ratio to the amount spent upon it or not?

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

That Rugby enthusiasts no more than Association supporters favour mid-week matches of secondary importance was proved on Wednesday by the small crowd which assembled at Swinton to witness che tie between Swinton and Runcorn in the first round of the lires,t Lancashire Border Cup competi- tion. Those who stayed away, however, missed a , very evenly and keenly-fought game, and a game, too, from which the home side only escaped a beat- ing by the skin of their teeth. At three-quarter time there Wd9 no scoring, and then the ball was run over the Swinton line. There was a tremen- dous struggle for possession, and there was some surprise when Referee M'Cutcheon allowed a try. However, a goal came,and this fairly put the Swin- ton men on their mettle, and it was a mighty relief to the home supporters when Morgan and then R Valentine scored. In the end, Swinton won by the very lowest margin.of one point. The forwards on both sides played with great determination, and the tackling on both sides had none of the half measure about it. For once in a way, the Swinton attack was pretty well held up, and though the home men had perhaps more method about them. they were doubtless greatly pleased when the whistle went and "all right" was signalled.

div.head: IMPORTANT STREET IMPROVMENTS AT WARRINGTON. Local Government Board Inquiry.
div.p: IMPORTANT STREET IMPROVMENTS AT WARRINGTON. Local Government Board Inquiry.

Colonel A. Gough and Clafe (representing the Ratepayers Assiciation.) THE WIDENING OF BRIDGE-STREET. Tne Tows CLERK mentioned th at the money was applied to be borrowed for 50 years. The INSPECTOR : When the purchase of tiff; pro- perty has 10,.en completed you will see your way to have a through street. The Tower.CLERK Tint is our intention. El DANGEROUS CORNER AL' BRIDGE Foot Mr, LONGDIN in referring to the purchase of Mr. Burgess's old shop at Bridgefoo'. said it was situated at one of the worst and most d ngerous corners in War- rington. The property came into the hands of a gentle- man who offered it to the Corporation and it was pur- chased by the Corporation for the purpose of widening Mersey-screet, and at some time or other of widening Warrington Bridge. This corner had been a source of danger for many years. ACADEMY-STREET IMPROVEMENT. Mr. LONGDIN nerc referred to the purchase of a shop at toe corner of Mersey-street and Academy-ir,reet for making an important widening at that point. WILDERSPOOL CAUSEWAY. Details were given of the purchase of property known as rwiss's property in Wilderspool Causeway, situated on the same side as St. James' Church but nearer to the Level railway croesing. This causeway, Mr. Longdin pointed out, had been widened to 601 t. for about a mile in length. The purchase of the property under discus- sion was to complete the widening of the road right into the town.

DIAL srREEr IMPROVENIENT. The hex', property brought under the consideration of the Inspector was the purchase of a block at the corner of Dial-street and Fennel-street. Mr GOUGH : Is it the intentioa of the Corporation to widen Dial-street. Mr LONODIN : Yes, it is proposed b make it 59 ft wide. The owners of the property wore goinc, to put this property in a thorough state of repair and if we had noti purcuased it at the time we did, we should have nad to pay three times the money for it when we wanted it. NEW STREET FROM BANK STREEf. Mr GOUGH Have you any idea of ccrrying this new street right through into Bridgt -street. 'fbe Tows CLERK: We should like to do so. Mr Gouda : It is very desirable. This improvement was next dealt with. Mr Longdie pointed out that it was formerly a very narrow lane leading to an important district. the owner wanted to make certain alterations, and he offer, d a strip of laud to the Corporation to make the lane 45 feet wide. Personal.

The interest of most people in the Belvoir Hunt (says the "Onlooker ") will centre round Lady Greenell, the bride of the Master. She is well- known in Cheihire as an excellent horsewoman and very fond of hunting. With a good seat and the best of hands, and a nerve that knows no shrink- ing, she should at once take a high place among the lady riders of the shires. Lady Greenell will have one immense advantage. She will be incomparably mounted. There is but one master of hounds who mounts himself and his men so well as Sir Gilbert , does In the splendid range of boxes which he built at Woolsthorpe-by-Belvoir,there are 65 horses, the like of which it would be hard to find in Eng. land, and well worthy of the best pack and one ot the best hunting countries in the United Kingdom. Each horse has a spacious box to himself, with electric light and water laid on. PATTISON AND PBRICINS for JAOKIITS, Golf." Capes, Macintoshes, etc.-17, SAroter-sTazET.—Advt. On Sunday the platform in the Bewsey-streeo Spiritutilist Hall was occupied by Mrs Nicholls, who in the afternoon gave clairvoyance and in the evens ing an address containing advice to investigators, followed by clairvoyance. On Monday evening the whole time was devoted to clairvoyant descrip- tions. On Tuesday evening Mr Will Phillips, editor of the" Two Worlds," dealt with a number of the written questions on the subject of Spiritualism, several of which formed the bases of interesting addresses, which elicited the applause of the audi- ence.

On Tuesday night an entertainment was given in connection with the Band of Hope. Mr. Hough presided, and gave a short address. The enter- tainment consisted of an excellent selection of limelight views, shown by Mr. Henry Taylor, Police Court Missionary. The story of "Christie' old organ" was shown, and the connective readings given by Mr. J. Wildman. A number of slides, illustrative of the soldiers of the Queen, &c., proved very interesting, and the juveniles were especially delighted with the comic slides. Hearty votes of thanks were given to Mr. Taylor and the reader. LADIBS BEST GLACE BOOTS AND—a-orr- UNDER T 1E CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREHT.-Advt. UNDER THE CLOCK FOR GOOD BOOTS. -Advt The Thomas Morris Charity. The. trustees of this charity, which is for the annual distribution of blankets and other warm clothing to old women over 60 years of age not in receipt of parochial relief, are the Rector of War- rington, the Rev Father Wilson, and Mr Browne, solicitor One husdred and eighty-six applications were received, and the trustees, atter carefully ex- amining them, decided to give a pair of blankets to all those old women who had not previously re- ceived blankets from the charity and flannel to the old women who received blankets two years ago. Toe other day ninety-nine pairs of blankets were distributed at the offices of Mr Browne, and twenty two parcels of red flannel. Many of the old women were disappointed, .but the trustees cannot give to any women in receipt of parochial relief.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
WARRINGTON PROVISION DEALERS PINED-AN INTERESTING CONTENTION. _ _ _

At the Warrington Peace Court on Monday, before the Mayor (presiding) and a full bench, Messrs. Kaye and Cowden, Forster-street. were Summoned for exposing a quantity of margarine, which was not labelled as re- quired by law, for sale. They were also summoned for selling margarine which was not placed in a proper wrapper, to a young woman named Elizabeth Jane Parker, and for selling botter which was adulterated 100 per cent with margarine.—lnspector Norman proved the first case—Cm's-examined by Mr. W J .Forshaw (who appeared on behalf of the defendants)the Inspector said that the margarice was nct visible to any- one entering the shop. If customers went to a certain counter they could see it.—Mr. Forshaw contended that the margarine must be exposed to the view of the cus— tomer and in this case it was not—The Mayor: You want us to believe, that it was not exposed for sale.—Mr. For- shaw : Yes. Tbo Mayor: Evon.if tne package was open P—Mr. Fondle a, again replied in the affirmative and proceeded to cite the Case of Crane v Lawrence in which it was decided by a metropolitan magistrate that unless the margarine was in sight of the purchaser It was not exposed for sale. It was held that if the margarine was placed behind a screen it was not ex- posed for sale. The decision was appealed against, but the Court ( f appal upheld it, the judges contending that the meaning of the Act was that if the article was ex- posed to view in the shop, a label mustte attached.— Mr. Forshaw read a detailed report of the case, and the Mayor said he coosidered that it did not go on all fours with the present case. The very important and vital point was that labels were fixed on a screen above the pareels and if that did not mean that the margarine was exposed for sale, he did not understand the facta.—Mr. Forshaw • We are told there were no labos upon them.—The Mayor: That is the offence.— Inspector Norman The margarine was in my sight when I was servcdo—The Inspector, in his evidence as to the other charges, said the young woman Parker went into the shop for a pound of tenpeony butter, and was supplied with what was certified by the public analyst to be margarine. It was delivered to her in plain paper.— The defence was that an assistant who ban only been in the emplay ef the defendants for three days, served the young woman with margarine in naistalia.—The magis- trates considered that the dcfendanra were legally responsible at-Ad imposed a penalty of 20. and costs in the cqsl of selling margarine as buttor.—ln the other cases defendants were fined in the WM.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.—Address by
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.—Address by

Councillors Bennett and Evans. Councillor Bennett presided at the meeting of Wycliffe P.S.A. !Society on Sunday afternoon. In the course of an address he said the Corporation was ex- antic what the people made it. When they found fault with tha Corporation they must remember that it was simply a reflection of themselves. For his own part he thought the present Warrington Corporation was one of the best Corporations they had had for many years and was doing some very usefial work. He appealed to his hearers to take an interest in the government of the town, for he held that if they did not do their duty as citizens, they were not going to do it as Christians. They could not serve their fellows better than by doing their duty to the town in which they lived. They had it in their power, in what-ver vocation they were placed, to prove their Christianity in a practi- cal way. It was their duty whether they were members of the Town Council or even , chimney sweeps to' do their best to make their work upright and honest so that it would stand. Some years ago Mr W T Stead wrote a book entitled "If Christ came to Chicago" ard they might also apply the same test to Warrington. If Christ came to Warrineton and visited Silver-.quare, Town Hill or some of those places did they think that He would say they reflected that spirit of brotherhood and love of one's fellows which He taught? Be thought not. There were many thing's in Warrington which were utterly contrary to Christianity. They needed less praying and singing and more practical Christianity. In nine points out of ten we were utterly removed from the true conception of a Christian city. After referring to the slums and streets full of drunken persons, and the black smoke in every civilised community he pointed out that it was the duty of everyone to bring about a condition of things more in harmony with Christian princlples.—Councillor Evans als, spoke and delivered an earnest address on " The Kingdom of Jesus Christ.' He observed that the brotherhood of that P.S.A. movement would be more effective as the spirit of Christ entered their hearts and minds. The world would become better as the indivi- dnat units of society became more Christlike. Miss Bridge very efficiently sang a couple of solos. The ser- vice was also taken part in by the Rev J Yonge, Mr George Wallington and Mr William Beswick.

Ball at the Winmarleigh Cafe. The usefulness and popularity of the Winmar- leigh Cafe has become so great that one wonders how it was possible, previously, to get on without it. On Tuesday evening the adaptability of the place was exemplified in another way, for a staff ball was held there, given by the directors of the Company. It was an immense success too. In the basement or crypt cf the caf6 there is vastly more space than anyone would imagine and the accom- modaricn for dancing is really excellent. The walls have been tastefully decorated, and adorned with innumerable Chinese lanterns, fans, so that the crypt now presents the appearance of a summer house in the land of the7celestials. No fault can he found with the floor, and the guests on Tuesday were loud in their praise of everything. Music was provided by Mr RII Pearson's popular orchestra, and a programme of 21 dances occupied the time very enjoyably between 8 p.m. and 2 a.m. In addition there were billiards, bagatelle,and other attractions, so that there was no excuse for allow- ing the time to drag on the part at any individual. Mrs Hay ward's catering was, of course, first class, and the arrangements in this department could not have been bettertd. This staff ball, so enjoyable in itself, ought to he the forerunner of many similar functions at the cafe, for no place is better suited for small parties and dances, where comfort and pleasure are the principal consideration.

div.head: Fatal Fall in a Bedroom.
div.p: Fatal Fall in a Bedroom.

Mr S Brighouse conducted an inquiry at noon on Tuesday, at the Warrington Police Station, respect- ing the death of Henry Thomas Nfoston, a stable- MC, aged thirty years, of Smith's Cottages, linuts- ford-road, Orappenhall, who died on Saturday morning from the effects of a fall in his bedroom on the same morning. Samuel Moston, brother, said that he deceased had been subject to fits for a number of years.—Ann Smith with whom the deceased had lodged, said that the latter had had four fits o'n the morning of the accident, and about 8.30 she heard a noise. On going to the bottom of the stairs, she found him lyingon his back with his head facing the bottom of the stairs. He was bleeding from a wound in the thigh. She sent for Police Constable Thomas, who attended to him. On going into the belro-en she fouu,l tha- aneth.then- ware vessel had been brokeri,'and no doubt this had been the cause of the wound.—Police-constable Thomas stated that be. rendered first aid. Though he arrived within a few rninutes the deceased had lost a large amount of blood owing to the artery in the thigh being cut. There was also a V-shaped piece of the utensil found in his shirt, near the place where the wound r7aB.—Dr Gomel' was sent for, and he took the deceased to the Infirmary. He had died before arriving at that institution.—A verdict of ".Acciden;al death " was returned and the coroner said that great credit was due to the constable for what he had done in the matter.

div.head: LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.

Smart Performance by Warrington. The Rochdale Hornets paid their annual visit to Wilderspool on Saturday, and brought a strong team in the hope of taking down the " Wirepullers," but, as usual; they failed. Up to Saturday the Hornets had only lost one watch in the Lancashire Senior Competi- tion whereas Warrington's balance was on the wrong side. Bate was the only absentee on the home side, Duckworth again filling the vacancy. Excellent weather favoured the fixture, but the crowd was not of the expected dimensions 4,000 being about the aggregate. M. M'Cutcheon (Oldham), was the referee and the teams lined out as follows : Warrington Hallam, full-back, Fish, Isherwood. Dickenson and Hockenhall, three-quarters; Burgess and Duckworth, half-backs ; Boardman, Morrison, Eden' Swift, Swift jun. Jolley, Scholtze and Aatrobus, forwards. Rochdale Hornets: Rigg, full-back; Wightman, Hickey, Field and Smith, three-quarters; Allen and Berrill, half-backs ; Langhorn Trembath, Howarth, Greenhalgh, Cooper, Cross, Hurst and Wilson, for- wards. Howarth started the game, and the visitors being early penalised Morrison gave Warrington a footing in their territory by a lofty free-kick. The ball came out of the pack on the home side and it was soon travelling towards the wing, Fish having bard luck in kicking dead when dribbling over. A touch kick landed the ball well under the posts, where Wightman saved his side by a clever mark. The Hornets were unable to clear their lines, Warrington keeping up an incessant and varied attack. Duckworth got away from the pack with a dribble and kicking past Rigg scored smartly near the posts. Fish landed an easy goal. Field then changed the venue with a dodgy run to centre where Jolley stayed further progress with a mark. Hallam was called upon as the result o. good footwork by the Hor- nets, but kept his charge intact. Bad passine from the pack lost the visitors numerous chances of making head- way. Warrington nearly always gained ground when they got the ball and from two smart passing move- ments Dickenson had hard lines in not getting a try. Every attempt by the Harnets to get away was frus- trated by the smart tackling of the home backs. Another raid of the visitors' goal near half-time doubled the score for Duckworth slinging the ball across to Fish,the latte dashed over, and placed a goal from a difficult angle Dickenson gave Hockenhall a pass soon after but Wight man safely held the right winger. Half-time: Warrington, 10 points; Rochdale Hornets, nil. Swift restarted and the Hornets took advantage of the wind to play on Hallam who was caught in possession. Warrington were soon retaliating and the forwards travelled down the field in a body Yield saving with a flying kick to touch near the line. Warrington heeled out well and Duckworth threw to Isherwood who drew the visitors on to Fish and slipped through himself very smartly. Fish missed the goal. Rachd tie showed signs of demoralisation now, and Warrington simply made rings round them. The forwards dribbled well up again and Burgess ming up scored the fourth try at the corner, Fish's kick at goal falling under the bar. The Hornets got close in and Allen attempted to score from a punt and rush trick, but Fish was there first and kicked dead. The effort was a mere flash in the pan, for Warrington drove the Hornets back. Isherwood speedily followed up his own kick and robbed Smith. Then followed a fine piece of play. The centre ran grandly till challenged near touch, when he tossed the oval across to Fish, who galloped round the posts with Rigg in close but vain attendance. The scorer also added a goal. yield did some good work after this, but was not supported, and Fish obliged with another brilliant run down touch, which would have been product.ve had bo not stumbled after 'ceating Rigg. Final : Warrington, 3 goals, 5 tries (21 points), Roch- dale Hornets, nil. Wigan v. St. Helens.

Warrington Just Win at Rochdale.

A tight 2ame was witnessed at Roadsle on Saturday, Warrington running out winners by a single point. The visitors had to defend almost immediately after the kick off. Grinarod, after a brilliant run scored at the corner tor the Hornets, the same player converting. Warring- ton pressed and Harris notched a try after a fine effort The Warrington three-quarters exhibited grand form which wm the hearty plaudits of the spectators A combined movement by the backs resulted in Harris scoring a second try, the goal kick failing. Half time arrived with the scors,Warrington two tries (six points) Rochdale one goal, one try (rive points). During the second half Warrington had the best of matters, Will- cocks soon scoring a third try. Ratcliffe's kick at goal was successtul. div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. Lancashire League.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. Lancashire League.
Eariestown v. Blackburn Rovers Reserve.

The visit of the Blackburn Rovers Reserve team to the Mesnes enclosure on Saturday, drew a crowd of more than average proportions, quite 800 people turning out to witness the match. Additional interest was c,mtred in the encounter when it became known that Oldham and Morgan had been left out of the first eleven and would therefore be playing with the Reserves. Besides these two notable exponents of the game, the visitors' team included five other first class men, as well as Knowles, who until quite recently kept goal for the first eleven, O'Brien, Iloilo, Spinks arid Kelly. The right back—Smith—is also a class man who has recently been signed on by the First Leaguers, and was being tried in this match. Altogether the Rovers had the best team they have turned out Co far this season. Earles- town were fully represented, Lee re-appearing at centre forward vice Linton. The visitors missed their train, and as a result, it was half-past three before the teams lined up in the following order : Esrlestown : Chew, goal ; Hayes arid Cottarn, backs ; Pennington, Green, and Clibtorn, half backs ; Bartley, Whitehouse, Lee, Leach, and Settle, fe: wards. Blackburn Rovers : Knowles, goal ; Smith and O'Brien, backs ; McClure, Spinks, and Bode, half backs ; Blackshaw, Dixon, Oldham. Morgan, and Kelly, forwards.

The afternoon turned out beautifully fine and the sun wag shining brilliantly when, having lost the toss, Lee started on behalf of Earlestown, against the wind and hill. The horne left were early prominent. trick; work by Settle taking play into the Rovers goal, but O'Brien easily got the leather away, and loose play on the part of Green left Oldham with a nice opening,. The visitors ceiitre however, dallied too hog, Hayes being on him before he could get in a shot which was easily negotiated by Chew. A moment later Oldham again got going and with a clear field, the downfall of the home goal appeared Imminent. Luckily for Earlestown, the centre fell over the bill in his eagerness to work himself into a nice posi- tion, but although on the ground with Hayes on top of him he cantrived to give Chew a warm handful to deal with Th. hall was at the other end in a trice, and ciever work by the home right resulted in Bartley swing- ing across a lovely centre, which Lee beaded in, Knowles just scraping the leather from under the bar. A short epell of mil-field play followed, after which tricky work by Leach left Settle with a perfect opening. The left winger made full use of his oppertunity as he dribbled the leather clese in and then gave Knowles no chance with a splendid shot which graz,d the bar and entered the far corner of the net: Encouraged by this success, which came after play had been in progress quarter of an her, the homestera very soon again made matters lively for the Rovers' defence. A correct centre from Settle left Whitehouse with an:Ep•n goal but greatly to the disgust of the home supporters, he lifted the leather yards over the bar. The Rovers attacked with great vigour and Chew was kept busily engaged, one
