div.head: COUNTY BOROUGH OF
div.p: COUNTY BOROUGH OF
WARRINGTON.
ELECTION OF MAYOR.
INTERESTING PROCEEDINGS.

At noon on Friday, the Warrington Town Council met and elected the Mayor for the ensuing year and conducted the annual business of the Council. Toere were present, the Mayor-elect (Alderman Roberts), Aldermen Fairclough, Sutton, Bolton Francomb, Shaw Green, Heaton, Hutchin- son ; Councillors, Monks, Plumpton. John Evans James Evans, F R Roberts, William Roberts, John Roberts, Smethurst, A Jolley, Manion, Bennett, Baird, Barton. Wilkinson, Peacock, Davies, Ellison, T J liaise, 3 Sampson,Rogers, with J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), S Wilson (deputy town clerk), T Longdin (boro surveyor), Dr Gornall (medical officer), C Madeley (librarian). There was a large attendance of the general public, including the Rev J and Mrs Yonge, Mrs Henry Roberts, Rev H G Roberts, It G Henshall, J Clayton (Liberal agent and W Holbrook (Conservative agent).

div.head: ELECTION OF MAYOR.
div.p: THE ELECTION OF MAYOR.

Alderman Fairclough was appointed to preside pro tem. Alderman SUTTON said it was his pleasing duty to propose the following resolution :—"That Henry Roberts, Esq., one of the aldermen of this borough, be and is hereby re-elected Mayor for the ensuing year, and until the acceptance of office by his suc- cessor." (Hear, bear.) Never, perhaps, in the tory of the Corporation, he observed, hike' the ques- tion of election of Mayor been more important than at the present time, nor had it been more necessary to exercise the greatest care and judgment in the selection of the gentleman to fill this important position. They had now attained to the more exalted position of a county borough,of whichAlder- manßoberts had the honour of being the first Mayor —(hear, hear) —and the work of the Corporation had increased during the last few years to an extent which the Council had never before experi- enced. Some of the extra duties which would be imposed upon the Corporation he might briefly mention. There was the supply of electric light and the construction of tram- ways in the borough, two new committees having been already appointed to undertake the conduc t of the work. There was the extension of the Infec- tious Diseases Hospital-. The present accommoda- tion had been found to be entirely inadequate for the requirements of the town. There would also be the erection of a small-pox hospital. That work, as they knew, had been reluctantly delayed from time to time because the Health Committee had not been perfectly satisfied with the proposed site at Pear Tree Farm; but now having had the offer of what they considered was a desirable site for the purpose they felt that this important work could no longer be deferred. The purchase of property for town improvement and the widening of the streets for tramways and for vehicular traffic, &c., the important work in connection with the water- works extension and the protection of their rights in connection with proper navigation of the river, were also questions of vital importance to the welfare of the borough which -you'd need the consideration of the Corporation. It would be seen , how very important it was that they should have a Mayor to preside over them who was highly qualified and competent in every respect to advise the committees and conduct all their ' negotiations in reference to these really important matters. He thought that from the opportunities they had had during the past year of witnessing the great ability displayed by the Mayor, they might congratulate themselves upon the fact that Alderman Roberts had consented to give his services for the benefit of the town for another year. ',Hear. hear.) Alderman Roberts had been been many times complimented upon the impartial manner in which he had filled the position of Mayor, and a good deal had been said at various times about how pleasantly they carried on the busi- ness of the Council. In fact they were a happy family. (Laughter) It was just as he said when he 'supported the resolu- tion that they should elect Alderman Roberts as mayor last year. He told them then they had only to put him in office to keep him quiet and compel him to behave himself. (Laughter). What he said had been fully carried out. The Mayor had conducted himself during the year in a very excel- lent way and had been perfectly impartial in every respect. (Hear, hear). Alderman MONIS in seconding the proposition said he had no doubt that not only among the members of the Council but among townspeople generally there was a feeling of great satisfaction at the prospect of having Aldermen Roberts to pre- side over the interests of the county borough for the ensuing twelve mouths. (Rear, hear.) The resolution was one he felt quite certain needed no wor.is of his to commend it to the members, and he would therefore leave it in their hands, feeling con- fident that it would have their unanimous approval.

Alderman FRA.NCOIfI3 sunported the resolution. He said he thought that Alderman Roberts had done well during the last year. He believed he would do equally well if not better in the c9ming year. (Meat, hear), He had brought to the conduct of the duties of the office a great amount of ability and hard work, and he (Alderman Francombl felt confident that during the coming year he would have every support from the members of the Cor- poration. It had not been mentioned that Alder- man Roberts had been wonderfully assisted by his wife and children. He hoped that Mrs Roberts would feel that she had conferred a good deal of pleasure upon them for the way in which she con- ducted her duties as Mayoress and the help she had given to her husband, (Hear. hear.) He had very great pleasure in supporting the resolution. The resolution was then put to the meeting, and unanimously carried with applause. Alderman FAincLouoK,accompanied by the pro- poser and seconder then proceeded to the Mayor's parlour to inform Alderman Roberts of his re-elec- tion as Nlayor. Shortly afterwards the ktayor re- entered the C mull Chamber and signed the usual declaration on acceptance of office.

THE MAYOR'S SPEECH. The Mayor,who was received with cheers,said : I be to thank you very sincerely and cordially for this signal expression of your confidence and appreciation of the work which I have etempted to do on behalf of this town during the pat year. I appreciate the honour, perhaps, even more fully than I did a year ago because Warrington has now assumed to the dignity of a county borough, and I have the great privilege as well as the honour of being the first Mayor of the county borough of Warrington. (Applause). I must also take this opportunity of expressing my very grateful thanks to the Town Clerk and to the other officials of the Corporation for the invaluable assistance I have received during the year which has gone by. Before making a very brief retrospective reference to the work of the town during the year which has expired I would like to express what I know is in the minds of every member of the Corporation, namely, our great regret at the removals which hare been caused and the gaps which have been created in our ranks by death during the past year. (flear,hear.) I shall not refer to them individually, to the gentlemen who have gone, but I think I may say without any hesitation that in regard to each one, and to all of nem, that they did what lay in them to the utmost of their ability to promote the interests of our town. (Rear, hear). I sincerely hope that the year upon which we have entered to- day will be free at any rate from gaps caused under such circumstances as those to which I have already referred. Ton remember that on the 9th November last year I did make some reference to the works in progress in which we were interested, or to the works I ought more properly to say, in contempla- tion. lam very glad to say in regard to most of them that what was then only contemplated has begus to be realised and that

CONSIDERIBLPI PROGRESS HAS BEON MADE. In regard to the Electric Light Supplythe cables for light ing the main streets havaltron laid, the works at How- lec have been practically completed as far as the build- ings are concerned; and the chairman of the committee had the pleasure to announce to us recently that he ex- pects to give us the electric light at any rate before Christmas. (Applause.) lam also informed that over 6.000 lights have already hoen applied for, which shows that the committee were justified in going on with that work, rand that we have every prospect of having a re- mundrative industry in our midst in this connec-ion be- fore long. In regard to the water works extens'ona I may say that all the contracts have been let ; the various works are being proceeded with ; the new main from Winwick to Appleton has been laid and that consi- derable progress has been made with the new reservoir at Winwick and also with the underground work in con- nection with it. In connection with
THE TRAMWAYS proposals the Bill I referred to in my brief addeyss fast year has become ourrframcvays Act;and we have decided to let the work as soon as tenders can bs obtained from

the Knutsford-roarl terminus to Warrington Bridge, up Bridge-street, Hylands-street, Palmyra-square, Winmar- leigb-street, Sankey-street to Sankey Bridges. Other portims will be taken in hand at the earliest convenient moment. In the meantime the application for light railways for outside diqtricts, seeking powers to run over our lines have had the most serious and continuous attention of the Committee, with the result that as at present advised the Committee cann9t grant such power to any applicant whatever. The work in connection with oar

div.head: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF TUB COUNCIL MARINE
div.p: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF TUB COUNCIL MARINE

This is another comparatively smaller matter which the Council might also consider during the ensuing year. We all know what inconvenience we are put to in meet- ing in this room and for reasons of healch as wall as comfort and convenience the Council may very properly consider the desirability of extending these premises to make them adequate for conducting the business carried on in them. These things will involve increased expen, diture but I aria glad to say in order to meet it. Ido not say entirely meet it, but I hope entirely meet it, we have a considerable income to look forward to. During the year ending September 1900.

OTTR RATEABLE VALUE HAS INCREASED by no less than £12,063, which represents a very large increased amount in rate contribution towards the expenditure of the Borough, We cannot expect that this increase, which is abnormally large, and brought about to a great extent by a re-valuation of the town, will he maintained in the same ratio, hut wa are satis- fied that our town will increasingly grow. The facili- ties which are offered for the development of trade and commerce are such that very few towns possess, and in a few years our population will be increased. Therefore I don't think anyone need be alarmed at the prospect of the large expenditure in front of us at the present tlme.The present rateable value of tho iinrough is £254,000 which is very considerably greater than two years ago. Further, in this connection, prnnerty brought into the Borough by the extensions of 1896 will on November 9th next year begin to make its contribu- tion of one-third to the improvement rate,so that thon two eircumstances.l think,justify me in suggesting that there is no need for alarm at the prospect of increasPd espanditare which still confronts us. (Clear, hear.) In conclusion, gentl6men may I say that these projasts in- volving a,s they do the expenditure of an enormous amount of money and representing not only our material, physical, educational and resthetic interests, prove in- contestably that we are
'CITIZENS OF NO ME&N CITY."

I hopfi and believe, that the feeling is growing amongst us that citizenship carries with it not only the inestimable privileges which the unsel- fish labours of those who " have gone before' have bestowed upon us, but also places upon our shoulders a like duty and responsibility in regard to those who have to follow on. Freely we have received and freely we should give. We are by no means yet an ideal town—our strAets might be cleaner, Vie environment of our large work;ng class population might be brighter, we want more Opel spans and opportunities of recreation, our artistic and education.' Ideals are still far from realisation, and yet in spite 04 many disadvantages, the future is full of promise and I cordially invite those amongst us who have leisure., sceial position and ability, to join with us in pressing forward those reasonable and necessary proposals which will make for the permanent improvement and con- tinued prosperity of our town and people. (Loud applause).

div.head: 'DEPU'ET-MAYOR AND MAYOR'S CELAPLAIN.
div.p: 'DEPU'ET-MAYOR AND MAYOR'S CELAPLAIN.

His Worship thin appointed Alderman Fairslougb deputy-mayor, and the Rev. John Yonge. Mayor's (than- lain. He explained that he intended visiting Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday morning, and the Parisb Church in the evening and hoped the arrange- ment would be as cardlally approved of as last year. They would, no doubt, have an opportunity! of receiving considerable profit from the attendance at both services. Alderman ScrTox anoounc6d that he should be unable to attend the services as he would be away from home.

Aldorman FAIRCLOUGH heartily thanked the Mayor for the honour he had conferred upon him in appointina him deputy-mayor. He could only say that he would endeavour rendlr his services to the Council to the best of his ability. THE RESIGNATION OF ALDERMAN HARRISON.

div.head: VACANCY FILLED.
div.p: THE VACANCY FILLED.

The MAYOR then moved a resolution expressing the regret of the Council at the resignation of Alderman Joseph Harrison. an honorary freeman of the borough, and placing on record its warm appreciation of the pub- lic services rendered by him during his connec- tion with the Council for upwards of thirty- six years. He remarked that it would not be consistent witn what was due to this fact, if he did not sty a word or two in support of the resolution. It was a matter of great regret to all of them that old age.with the failing of physical powers, which evidently followed it, had rendered it no longer possible for Alder- man Harrison to be amongst them and give them the benefit of his advice and assistance. A man like him who had been for over 36 years a member of the Council was entitled to more than a mere formal resolution in recog- nition of his services. He (the Mayor) was glad to see that the Council honeured Alderman Harrison by appointing him Mayor in the years 1883-4-5 and 6, a Justice of the Peace in 1886, and a freeman of the borough in 1897. He moved the resolution with very considerable &Tarot.

Alderman SUTTON, in seconding said he quite agreed with the remarks of the Mayor. There was no doubt that in years gone by Alderman Harrison was a very valuable member of the Corporation and reniered very great szrvices for the town. The resolution was unanimously carried. _ . _
The qii3t2 th-in declarqi the offici of an alderman to be vacant and invited the Council to nominate a successor to Mr Harrison.
Vo ing priers were handed round and when they had been collected and examined it was found that every

div.p: Imember of the Council had recorded his vote in favour ot Councillor Fred-rick William Monks. The MA.Yog said he had very great pleasure in declar- ing that Councillor Monks had been unanimously elected an Alderman of the borough, and, at the same time took the opportunity of offering him his sincere and hearty congratulations. (Applause.) Councillor MorsKs then signed and read the usual declaration and afterwards thanked the Council most cordially for this further honour they had conferred upon him by electing him an Alderman of the borough. He did so with a feetine, of regret that he should have been selected under such circumstances, owing to the unfortunate resignation of Alderman Harrison. He should like to take this opportunity of expressing his sympathy with him and he was sure he was only ex- pressing the sympathy of the whole Council with him in the sad circumstances in which he had felt it necessary to resign. With regard to the pesition,Alderman Monks remarked that it tir4A new ten years since he became a member of the Ceunetl and at rather an unusually early opportunity the Unreel' placed their confidence in him by electine him to the position of chairman of a com- mittee. Ho had always felt that it was a laudable ambition to do one's work in such a way as to deserve the respect and esteem of his fellow members, and he had always tried to earn that respect and esteem. He had a sort of feeling that day that although it was now somewhat of a formal metter to appoint the senior councillor to the position of alderman he still thought there was a personal ele- ment in it, which obtained in his case. (Hear hear.) He felt that to some extent they might be otherwise influenced and that it was a pleasure to them to appoint him Si that position. (Applanse.) This made it all the more acceptable to bim and he could only again thank them for the additional honour. In times past he had had to place himself upon the in- dulgence of the Connell and invite their c mfidence , and he did not remember a single case in which he re ally wanted their confidence that they refused to give it him (Hear, hear.) This made the honour more acceptable and he thanked them most cordially for having con- ferred it upon him. (Apolause.) APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEES. The meeting then proceeded to the appointment of committees, when the alterations made at tbe caucus meeting were coefirmed. RE CU RNING OFFICERS. Councillor SMETHURST moved that the undermentioaed aldermen he appointed returning officers for the various wards :—Town Rail Ward, Alderman Reberte ; White- cross Ward, Alderman Monks; Bewsey Ward, Alderman Faircloueh ; Orleei Ward, Alderman Hutchineon ; St. John's Ward, Aldertnan Sutton; Fairfield Ward, Alder- man Heaton; Howley ceard, Alderman Francemb ; St. Austin's Werd,A.lderman Shaw Green ; Latchford Ward, Alderman Bolton. Councillor A JOLLEY seconded and the motion was carried unanimously. WARRINGTON'S REPRESENTATIVE ON THE ASYLUM'S BOARD. The MAYOR said they had &reedy expressed their unanimous aereetnent that Alderman Feancomb should be appointed to represent Warrington oa the Lanca- shire Asylums Board as he had boon the representative on the County Council for so long. Aldermen SHAW GREEN seconded the motion which was unanimously agreed to. This concluded the business of the meeting.

div.head: NEW POLICE BUILDING&
div.p: NEW POLICE BUILDING&

have been well advanced, and the architectural features so far disclosed promise a very handsome structure. It is to be haped we shall be in occupation before this municipal year expires; and in this connection may I suggest that when we cease to use the old Police Court that the old premises shall be taken dawn and an open space created,furnished with a few convenient seats and beautified as far as possible by the planting of suitable trees. (Applause.) I feel certain—and I am extremely gratified with the way you have received my proposal— that the suggestion if carried out will resuit in a very desirable improvement at a very low cost. (tiear, bear.) With regard to the comstion of

PUBLIC MALT we have entered upon the enlargement of the Infectious Diseases Hospital. The new pavilion will soon be com- pleted and the administrative block commenced: The land necessary for the erection of a sanatorium at Sankey has been provisionally acquired,and the plans have been approved and we hope very soon to be able to remove by these measures the odium which has attached to us for so many years of being insufficiently prepared to meet any serious epidemic of that dreaded scourge. small-pox. (Hear, hear.) The widening of Knutstord- road has to a large extent been accomplished, and we hope very soon to be able to carry the work to a further point. Councillor Ellison will admit that some little has been done in the direction in which he takes such an active interest—in the opening to the public of Tictoria Park.one of the most desirable purchases which has ever come into the possession of the Corporation (Applause.) I think every facility will be furnished shortly for the extended use of that desirable prop-rty. The plans for the Turkish'Baths have been passed'eand an application is now before the Local Government Board for power to borrow money for the purpose of erection. The

div.head: NEW TECHNICAL SCEIGOLS
div.p: NEW TECHNICAL SCEIGOLS

are becoming a thing of substance. They are now past, the experimental stage so far as the proposals for new buildings are concerned, and the committee who have had charge of this matter, having given the most care- ful attention to it will come before us very shortly for our approval to a definite scheme, the plans of which to a certain extent have beeq carefully considered. (near hear.) I should like to say a word or two alalut the

MUCH CRITICISED BRIDGE-STREET IMPROVEMENT I hope gentlemen I am not wearying you with these remarks ; they are intended not entirely for this Corp.or- stion as a Corporation, but for our friends outside who have not the same facilities as we have here of hearing from time to time exactly what position we stand in. This s -,heme is necessarily making but slew progress, but on Wednesday wit a Local Government Board Inspector will hold an inquiry here for the purpose of our borrowing £60,000 for street improvements the bu'k of which is required for the portion of Bridge-street f:om Friars Gate to Rclands-etreet. We have also had a valuation prepared, and others are in progress of the property required for the completion of the w idenins up to Market Gate. It is desirable to explain th at one of the principal reasons which makes progress necessarily STOW is the difficulty of dealing with valuable businesses carried on in the shops required with as little injury as possible to the pro- Poetors of such businesses. I need only point out the fact that many occupiers who have built up busi- nesses at considerable expense and labour extending over many years and are not themselves owners of the pro- perty required for this improvement would be in Emmet cabs almost ruined if this Council did not show them the utmost possible consideration in regard to the enforned removal which this improvement makee necessary, and I hope that critics outside will bear this important fact in mind—that it is not besiuse we desire to make slow progress, but that it is that we wish to take into the fullest possible consideration the interests —inNoine cases the vital interests—of the occupiers o the premises which we require. (Applause). I sbal only refer very briefly to the

PURCHASE OF THE SPRINGFIELD PROPERTY which I bope we shall add to the Queen's Gardens and so make that very pleasant little district, so far as the present gardens are concerned; larger and consequently more ris;ful than it is at present. Daring the year we have also receive] the handsome gift from Sir Peter Car- lacy Walker, which adds much to the appearance of these Town Hall premises. Taere still remains amongst a number of other things one more pressing question, and that is how we are to deal with

WARRINeTON BRIDGE. (Hear, hear.) We have called iu as you are aware Mr. John James Webster, a Warrington man bred and born, about whose ability there is no questioo,to advise us on the matter and he has submitted two proposals which will come before you for consideration, One is the pro- posal to widen the present bridge by throwing out canti- levers and the other proposal is to build a new bridge entirely. My own opinion is that the first proposal which is moderate in expense will be found in a very short time to be utterly insufficient for the purpose. That is a matter the Council will consider when it comes before it. (Applause.)

div.head: FIX TURES AND SCORES.

Letter to the iter.
Canon Wood and "Ignorant Runcorn."

Sir,—As an old resident of Runcorn I was puzzled at ' first to know who W, H. Stables, Runcorn, was ; then I remembered that there was an electioneering agent of that name in the town about two years ago. but I always thought he lived at Weston. If he is the !same person I think be should at least be careful to give his address correctly before he charges me with not daring to sign my name. Bat perhaps he wrote the letter at the Vicarage at the dictation of Canon Wood, hence the mistake in the address, It is a very "gentlemanly "way of putting things for him to say that because I imputed words to Canon Wood that he never used I am "most ignorant." I certainly I expected better logic from Mr. Stables. It might imply 1 unfairnesq, but certainly not ignorance. I did not hear Canons Wood's speech therefore could not see that it was meant for a joke, but I know several of my friends who heard it were very much annoyed at its cynical tone. I based my remarks on the newspaper report which certainly does not contain many" laugh- ters " except when Canon Wood mentioned how the old organ had been proselytized. It was very fine strategy on Mr. Stables' part to call it a joke, tfut let me remind him of the fable about the Ads stoning the frogs ; what was fun to the lads was death to the frogs, and in this case what was fun for the Masters of Arts was instil- iugEto those criticised. Because if it were meant for a joke, bow is it the Canon repeats his jokes so often ? I have beard him speak in the same strain before, and there is an old saying that " Cabbage isn't good boiled twice." Mr Stables wishes me to treat the whole speech as a joke, and yat in the very next paragraph of his letter he himself treats it seriously. He is very emphatic in one sentence, and then begins a later one with an " if," when you know you are in the right it is not necessary to use an " if." Will Canon Wood please explain what be meant by the expression "They had an intelligence of a kind ' and "the intelligence was represented by the school teachers." II Canon Wood had stopped after speaking about- -1 the wealth of the town I should have let that pass with out notice. but I felt bound to enter my protest against the remarks about our intelligence; _ _ .

It is too bad of Mr. Stabice dragging in the Technical Institute, but as he has mentioned it, will he kindly ask the Canon how many Committee Meetings he has at- tended during the last three years ? Has he attended three times in the last three years. I remember that Canon Wood was at one time a member of the Board of Guardians. Did he withdraw because he felt lonely in not having any churchmen to keep him company ? If Mr. Stables had substituted " interests of the church" for" interests of the town "then I could have agreed with him.
"ONE OF THE IGNORANT."

div.head: Runcorn Football Club and
div.p: Runcorn Football Club and
Committee Tickets.

Sir,—l was pleased 'when I read " Fairplay's " letter, in your issue of N member 9. lam glad someone has at last seen the doings with the tickets, that should be given to the committee. lam a member of the Run- corn FO3: ball Club and am only a working man, and I think, go away with the team (and I am proud of such a set of players) as often as any other follower. I agree with " Fairplay "and so will every other working man that it is a great expense, and is a slight never to be offered a ticket. It would look as if we were acknow- ledged as members, but when non-members get them it is slighting us beyond measure. Only this season the team were going away and the secretary was asked for a ticket. Of course, he had none, and the member took his word. Shortly after that I know there were tickets given away. I may tell the committee they will find the members, although only working men will not stand by and see the tickets given to one clique.—Yours, A MEMBER.

div.head: Resignation of Alderman Higginbottom, Manchester.'
div.p: The Resignation of Alderman Higginbottom, Manchester.'

Sir.—Having noticed your reference to th 3 Manches• ter City Council and Mr Lloya Iliggiohottom, I shall feel obliged if you will permit M 3 to dtate that a Town Councillor who has a business is not allowed to trade with the Corporation, because his personal interests in business with the Corporation might be detrimental to the ratepayers and would I believe be illegal. But if a Town Councillor is a !Arg,e shareholder and Director of a limited company, it is I believe, legal for him to do busitets with the corporation through that company, though I do not think that it is desirable, for under such conditions he might be unabln to serve two masters, and there weuld be great danger of him sacri- ficing the interests of the ratepayer-, to promote the business of a company of which ha was D rancor. Laws make things legal or illegal but cannot change the wrong to right. Stealing would be wrong whethar there was a law forbidding it or not. I think it is very undesirable for a Councillor to trade with the Corpora- tion either as an!individual or through a limited liability , company, for if goods were supplied that were not satisfactory and an official found fault with them it might I fear in some cases cause that official to lo us place A councillor might also he tempted to advocate the past- ing of measures not so much becatpe he thought thee would be beneficial to till public as because he expected they would benefit a company in which he might be greatly interested. A corporation ought to be free from suspicion and should act both legally and justly to- be worthy of respect. Theae who desire to do right do net often want to be trusted. Sametimes people take part in public life prompted by Ambition, vanity, and greed, and with tyranny, bribery and corruption in one war or other they may succeed. To disregard the maimed and blind, and the public in the put wit of selfish objects is about as mean a thing as any man can be guilty of, and if the eyes of everyone could be opened, those Who do so might bide themselves for everrnore.—Yours &3., S. KENYON. Warrington, November 15th, 1900:

div.head: Lord Methuen in Action. ---- Porn-Porn Captured.
div.p: Lord Methuen in Action. ---- Porn-Porn Captured.

Methuen came across a body of Boers on the 10th Inst., while on the march to Lichtenbuurg. They fled when his troops came to close quarters, and in the pursuit we captured a porn-porn. Piet Lem- mer, cousin of the commandant of that name, died at Lichtenburg on the 10th inst., from wounds received the previous day. A police post near Vyrburg, which was attacked on the 10th inst., suc- ceeded in killing several Beers and capturing two wounded prisoners, one of whom is Field-Cornet Duplessis. The police had three men wounded. One has since died.
Ladysmith's Claims against the Military.
PIETERMARITZBURG WEDNESDAY.

The Town Council of Ladysmith has been in- formed by the military authorities that a claim of £2,911 for rations supplied to the townspeople dur- ing the siege by the military authorities will be waived, but that the Council's counterc:aim for wood used by the garrison amounting to over £l,OOO, will not be paid, The Council will appeal to Lord Roberts.

div.head: Letter from Major Adam. ---- Farewell to the Volunteers. CatlV. Kipje, near Blood River, _ Mouday, 15th October, 1900.
div.p: Letter from Major Adam. ---- Farewell to the Volunteers. CatlV. Kipje, near Blood River, _ Mouday, 15th October, 1900.

The Mayor of Warrineton has received the following letter frem Major Adam Ist South Lancashire Regiment. Dear Mr. Rsberts,—l have to think vou for your kind and welcome letter of September 7th, which reached me a few days since. Pray forgive pencil, but my ink has " given nut," and I sin reduced to this. My first news is that Captain Appleton and his merry men left us, at very short not:ce, on Setureay (two days ago). They only got criers for home on Friday evening, and were to meals Dundee yesterday. To-day they will probably rail to Pietermaritzburg, and before many days, lucky fellows, will be on the briny with their nosed' pointing homewaris. We all envy them horribly, but still they deserve their luck. They have been an excel- lent lot. and I can write with some knowledge of them as I had them on detachment with me during part of June, all July, and August. Of course. Captain Ap eeton is now a friend of some 13 years standing, and I long ago coeceived a very warm regard for him. Latterly he has been sharing my tent, and I never want a better cemoanion. I have never seen him look en well, or sleep and eat so heartily as he has done out here, and lam sure he has benefited very greatly in every way. It has been a great pleasure to have him and the men with us. They all showei a mast excellent and willing spirit throughout in hard and easy times equally. and Ido think alai tro4t that now the misunderstand lags and mistrust which existed some time ago amongst a few people in Warrington with regard to soldiers, may be removed by this amalgamation of Reenters and Volun- teers. You, I know, have been very largely instrumen- tal in helping to this end. I assure you we value your kindness very highly. Appleten left at 4 a.m., and as he had to march past my kopjs (I am about 2i miles west of the Divisional Camp, with half &battalion guard- ing the flank) I get up and rode with him about two miles to bid him and his men good-bye. There was an extremely happy look in their faces. lam glad you saw my letter in "To Day" anent the allegation that the Snith Lancashire's had failed to follow their officers. I have now received a complete apology fern the Cor- respondent of the paper. I trust that " To-day " has already given it as wide a circulation as it did the original calumny. It was a cruel, though m'staken and inadvertent thing to put in print. You may ask what we ere doing just now ? Well, the fragments of our Division (for we have left garrisons at Wakkerstroom, Utrecht, and Vrigheid) are sitting here by the Blood River, half way between Utrecht and Vrigheid. scouring the country, watching Boer Laagers in the Bellelae Bergen to the north of usswhere there are still considerable numbers of them, escorting convoys of food and stores to and from Vrigheid, etc., etc., but the "elusive " Boer will not come down and fight. Be sits up in the hills and" snipes " intermittently when the chance offers. It is such a feeble form of resistance t hat I believe it must shortly die a natural death. Yet he is capable of nothing higher. We made a great mistake in not pushing on into Vrigheid on a certain Tuesday. about a menth sines, when we shelled the enemy off Scheepers Nek, six mile; from the town. Had we pushed on for we had some 5,000 men, of whom between 2,000 and 3,000 were mounted, we should have bagged the whole of the Vrigheid Commando. I am enclosine a characteristically "slim "letter from a rebel Natal Boer, who after being under our Regime for many peeve, willingly formed the endeavour to "throw the English into the sea," and fought against us He has been condemned to three years imprisonment and a fine So he indites the enclosed letter to the " Natal Witness." This is a tree piece of Boer charac- ter, having deliberately violated his obligations he prays the Deity to be merciful to those who testified to his treachery. I fear the whole nation Is steeped in tee same hypncrisy, with very few exceptions. The Boers cheat each other readily, and regard it merely as a smart stroke of business. I tried a rich B )e- merchant the other day by Court Martial in Vrigheld for having Manger rlfis3 csncealed in his premises after surrendine to the British and swearing solemnly he had given uo all arms. He swore solemnle before the Court he did not know a rifts was there. We condemned him to a £25 fine and 84 days' imprisonment, with hard I boor. He was removed to Dundee next morning, and sent me a message by two different officers to say he was " deeply grateful to me for my leniency, as be had expectee a sentence of 10 or 12 year?, but he was innocent." I was rather amused at the gratitude which was more signi- ficant of guilty expectancy than anything else. Now, must say good-bye. Kind remembrances awl all good wishes to old friends in good old Warrington. Yee will doubtless give a triumphant welcome to your Vce- unteers. I trust they may find you serving aa c mti term as Mayor, for I know how much you have done for the :town in your term of office, ad I hose you may not once, but often, find yours,lf in the honourable, though arduous position. We in the old 40Th. have no,; forgotten the great kindness with which you helped ias in regard to clothing, etc, for the men of South Lane-- shire serving our here,
Yours very Eineerely, F. A. Adam. The following is a elpy or the letter referred to by Major Adam.

div.head: HONOUR FOR A WARRING-
div.p: HONOUR FOR A WARRING-
TON lAN.
First Mayor of Bethnal Green.

The "Bethnal Green News" of Novernbor 10% alludes to the recent election of Mr Felix Loughlin as the first Mayor of Bethnall Green. It will be remem- bered that Mr Leuehlin, whe is a Roman Catholic, was at one time a j .weller carrying on business in Butter- market-street, and that he was for some years a mem- ber cif the Board of Guardians. He was PresLient of the Warrington Branch of the Irish National League for many years, and up to the time he left Warrington. ills Irish blood, says the newspaper in qsestion, found the cause of the Irish Nationalist movement sufficiently attractive for him as to enlist not only his symeathies, but his weir. After a quarter of a century spent in Warrington he removed to London, and started as a licensed-victuelter in Barnet-Grove, Bethnal Green. That was eight years ago. Some little time after he ' had been there, the Local Government Act, reconstitu- Jing the' vestries, came into operation, and Mr. 'Loughlin found himself standing on the Radical ticket a.s'a candidate. It N 4 as as a Racl,cal he first entered the vestry just over seven years ago, and a consistent Radical he has remained ever since, a man of more than ordinary ability,an able spe4ker, and one in a position to give the time necessary for the proper discharge of his duties, Such was the colleague the Bethnal Green Vestrymen found in Mr. Loughlin, and they were not slow o recognise his abilities by promoting him to the ch irmanship of one of the committees. Since then he has 03ennied the positions both of Church- warden and Overseer, and in May, of 1898, he received the blue riband of the vestry, in the shape of the chairmanship—the highest office it was in their power to give him. The eosition of chairman of the vestry, carried with it also—as does the new honour of Mayor—tho honourable office of Justice of the Peace, and during the time that Mr. Loughlin was on the Bench of magistrates for the Tower Hamlets division, he gained the respect and esteem of all his colleagues for the extremely fair and impartial way in which he always acted. After 1898 Mr Loughlin retired to the humbler 'rank of Vestryman, but now that the opportunity has come again f n. the members of the first Borough Council Ifr Bitten( Green to reward good and faithful service, [honestly and conscientiously rendered, by the bestowal lof the high offl le of first Mayor of the Borough of BPthnal Green, it is to Mr Loughlin again that the honour has gone. Mr Loughlin is married, and is the father of a family of nine children. His wife is ex- tremely well known also throughout the district as a memper of the Bethnal Green Board of Guardians. Mr Loughlin is not a man fond of display of any kind, and even if he were in the position, it is doebtful whether he would be in favour of any lavish expenditure as Mayor. That he will discharge the duties of his high office faithfully and well, and with dignity to the borough, goes without saving. It is equally sure that he will not, by any inordinate display or unwarranted expenditure,- set an example as first Mayor of Bethnal Green. which it will be difficult for a humbler colleague to follow. Mr Loughlin has pledged himself to only re- tain the office for one year, and moreover, he has de- clined to allow any salary to be attached to the position. We extend the heartiest of good wishes to his Worship, Felix Loughlin the first Mayor of the Borough of Bethnal Green. ,

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.] LIOENSING REFORM,
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.] LIOENSING REFORM,
BY THE HON. SIDNEY PEEL.
The Tied House System.

The tied house system is not a new creation of recent years. As long ago as 1818 a select com- mittee of the House of Commons reported very strongly against the effects of the tied, or as it was then called, the" bound" house system. The beer house legislation of 1830 to which later reference will be made was partly an attempt to break it down; while Mr. Villier's committee of 1854 actu- ally went so far as to recommend free granting of all licenses wit the same object. But it is only of late years that the system has begun to spread at such an eitraordinary rate as to make it a most prominent feature in any survey of the drink prob- lem in England. At the present time probably at least 75 per cent of the on-licensed houses are tied, and even the off- beer houses are falling more and more into the hands of the brewers. In Manchester about 90 per cent. of the houses are said to be tied. In Sheffield, in 1897, of 523 fully licensed houses 443 were tied and 75 free; of 650 beerhouses, 467 were tied and 183 free. In the police district of the county of Lan- caster about the same time. 1,569 out of 2,297 fully licensed houses,and 1,417 out of 1,861 on beer houses were tied, as well as 453 out of 986 off beer houses. In Chester the figures were 80 per cent. of all licenses tied. In Staffordshire in 1896, there were of fully licensed houses, tied 1,177, free 837; of beer houses (off) tied 137, free 232. In Liverpool, where the manager system prevails, there were in 1892, 1,057 licensed houses belonging to brewers occupied by paid managers, 218 occupied by tied tenants of brewers, 136 by tenants of private owners, and 667 by private owners them- selves holding the license A great many similar figures might be quoted from other parts of the country; these are enough to give some indication of how widely the system prevails, and the propor- tion of tied houses is increasing every month.

div.head: WHY THE SYSTEM DEVELOPS,
div.p: WHY THE SYSTEM DEVELOPS,

The reasons for this developmegt are principally to be found in the conditions of the brewing trade. Brewing has fallen more and more into the hands of brewers for sale, and home brewing is almost a thing of the past; owing to the improvement of the methods of brewing publicans have found it cheaper and better to get their beer ready made from the brewer, than to brew it themselves. The number of public brewers, and the size of their breweries has increased very much, and conse- quently there has been great competition among them to secure channels for their trade. Probably the better brewers would_ have been very glad to

let things remain on the former plane of free com— petition, but as other brewers have bought up and tied a number of houses, they have found them— selves compelled to do the same. This has led to a great struggle to secure houses for the sale of their goods, and prices have been forced up to an almost incredible extent; in fact there has been what is called the public-house boom, It would have been impossible for the brewers to raise the vast sums ' necessary for this purpose had it not been for the extension of the company system, and there arises the double consequence that an immense amount of capital has been put at the back of the drink traffic, and that large numbers of the public have becomely directly interested in maintaining its profits The tied house system has in this manner become by the necessities of circumAances, rather than by any inherent viciousness in this particular relationship between a brewer and a tenant, a great obstacle in the path of any reform. The influence of the large capital which has been invested is seen in many directions; the instrument of distribution must be sharpened up and made a effective as possible, for by some means or other a return has got to be obtained for the monies ex- pended. A tumble-down old house is furbished up, perhaps re-built and made as attractive as possible; a house doing no business is kept going, when it might otherwise be abandoned, in order to barter it against the gift of a valuable new license in a new quarter. The houses must be kept open for sale as long as possible. Thus an agreement between brewer and tenant at Birmingham contained a clause by which the tenant bound himself "not to close or permit the house to be closed during hours in which the same may by law be kept open, or do or permit or suffer any act whereby the custom and business may be less,.ned or injured" In other words the tenant was not to be allowed to close on Sundays or earlier on week days, even if he himself desired to do so. Similarly in Cheshire, in 1892, out of 47 houses having six day licenses (a license to sell on six days only at a reduced duty, granted only when voluntarily applied for) 43 were free houses, though tied houses were in the majority in the county. Such a clause as that quoted is a very natural one in the interests of the brewer, who gets his return for his money by the amount of beer consumed in the house, but it illustrates the posi- tion which the owners of tied houses must be expected to take up towards any reform which would tend "to lessen or injure the custom or business."

div.head: EFFECTS OF THE SYSTEM
div.p: EFFECTS OF THE SYSTEM

The effects of the tied house system cannot, how- ever, be summed up in a general phrase. There is a arett deal of conflicting evidence as to its results in different parts of the country, but before going further it will be best to desc-ibe the different systems of tying. In London the brewer usually holds a mortgage on the house, and in consideration of the loan, the lease holder, or owner, of the premises agrees to , take from him all malt liquors; perhaps there is a second mortgage on the house with a similar clause I tying for spirits. Elsewhere the brewer generally holds the freehold or a long lease of the premises, and puts in a tenant usually on a yearly tenancy at 6, 3 or 1 month's notice, but sometimes at less Sometimes the brewer merely puts in a manager, who is paid a wage, and is liable to dismissal like any other servant Thus the occupier of a tied house shades down by imperceptible degrees from the freeholder, whose premises have been mort- gaged to a brewer, to a weekly tenant at a nominal rent or a mere paid manager. The important thing which they all have in common is the tie. The stringency of the tie varies very much; sometimes the tie is for beer only, sometimes for beer and spirits, sometimes for every article that can be used in a public-house The occupier of a tied house at Hull was reported to have said, "I am tied for every d--d thing but sawdust" Now in the case of a good and conscientious brewer, who took care to treat his tenants fairly, and did not; abuse the obligation under which they lie to him, there might be no particular harm in the system: the tied houses might be superior in con- duct to the free, if the brewer kept a strict outlook and did his best to prohibit all doubtful practices Unfortunately the brewer is not always content with the profits he derives from the wholesale trade in beer, but is anxious to take some of ti,e retail profits as well—in other words he charges more to a tied customer for the goods which he is bound to take, than to a free, sometimes as muci as 104. a barrel of beer more. Such a burden may and does become very severe, if the tenant is tied for all articles. It is true that in return for this the rent is often lower to a tied tenant than to a free (and a good many public houses are rated too low for this reason). But this difference does not usually com- pensate for the difference in the price of beer There is no reason why the arrangement should be made except that the tenant has to sell more beer in order to make the same profits as before, and p,obably a brewer would not be long content with a tenant who took advantage of the lower rent and let down sales.

Thus in a district wherelicenses are numerous the tied publican i ground between the millstones of external competition and internal pressure. The temptation to push the trade onduly is very strong • he has probably sunk his little all in the house and cannot afford to leave ;he must sail as near the wind as he can; if he does not push the trade enough, he is in danger of losing his tenancy ; if he pushes it too much, he is in danger of being detected in a breach of the law; in which case he will be instantly turned out by the brewer, and he may have even signed a blank application form for a transfer, which only wants the date and name of the trans- feree to be filled in.

Probably competition is generally too keen for a brewer to 'find it worth his while to put his tenant off with inferior liquor; in districts where one brewer has a practical monopoly there might be a temptation to do so, and the public might in such a district be under some grievance through b-ing able to obtain the beer of one' brewer only.

But such localities are not common, and com- plaints as to the qua,ity of beer supplied are few. Another complaint is perhaps better founded, that inasmuch as the sale of liquor is more profitable than that of other kinds of refreshment,tied houses tend more and more to become mere taps for the
sale of liquor, so that it is "often difficult to obtain any food or even a cup of tea in them, and the term licensed victualler becom2s a distinct mis- nomer.

Anything that tends to make the position of the license holder more precarious makes him more likely to violate at any rate the spirit of the law; but, it may be asked, if the tenant is to be sub- jected to hard conditions, how is it that he enters upon his tenancy at all; brewers and their agnts do not take him by the throat and force him to sign an agreement; it is a voluntary act on his part. The ex- planation lies in the fact that to a certain class of people a public house is a!sort of El Dorado,in which all their little savings may be profitably invested, and in the management of which the rest of their lives may be securely and pleasantly passed. The justices' clerk of Bristol spoke before the Royal Commission of houses (happily exceptional) that were mere traps to catch the savings of thrifty poor people. Another witness said that the tenants at Sheffield were often thrifty sober people,who thought the public louse a good investment. They came chiefly from the neighbouring villages, put them- selves into the hands of the brewers' agents, and made no inquiry as to the fate of the past occu- pants; in a few years they found it a bad specula- tion and left in debt.. So at Chesterfield the tenants were often miners with a little money who dreamt of a fortune by taking a public-house. The large number of transfers. (i e from nne
license-holder to another) among tied-houses points to the conclusion that there must be something wrong in the system. In Leeds the transfers in one year amounted to—
Of fally-licensed houses .... tied 54 1 out of total free 311 353. Of beer houses ... ... tied 72 1 out of total _ _ free 46 f 410.

... tied 391 out of total free 325 401. and this, when the free houses in Leeds were still more than twice as numerous as the tied. The jus- tices' clerk of Birmingham, not at all unfavourable to the tied system on other grounds, admitted that the large number of transfers showed "that the tenant cannot make it pay, and is glal to get out. and the brewer is glad he should go out iu order that a man with more enterprise should make a trade."
Of shops
This frequency. of transfer, and the ease with

which the licenging authority allow transfers to be granted, no inquiry being made into the reason of the transfer, as long as a satisfactory character is forthcoming for the ingoing tenan., is a grea- in- s rumen t in the hands of the tied house owner.

We have already noticed the blank application forms for transfers which are some• imes signed by the tenant, when he goes into the house: The con- ditions of the agreement make it generally possible for the brewer to get rid of his tenant on the firs' hint of an offence against the law. It is argued that this has the effect of making the system even more stric in enforcing order than the law itself, for immediately the law is broken, the tenant is removed, and a new tenant wit,h a good charac'er put in without any trouble But it too often happens that a tenant, who Comes in with a good character goes out after no long time with a bad (:te, and so the sams process goes on, but. the house r -mains. Of course it is an advantage that a had tenant should be renr,ved, but. the fact

that the house has been badly conducted is lost sight of in the proc-,53 ; even a conviction is often thought to be ourged by a transfer, and the chsnce of extinguishing a bad house is lost In fact the licensing justices entirely abr)gate their functions, arid hc 'me s m•Are court for registering the decrees of tla, br-w,+r-. In some places the police even rep)rt to the brewer owners anything that they may have observed going wrong in the house in order that the tenant may be quietly re- moved, and do not mention the fact to the licens- ing authority to whom the license holder ought to be primarily responsible. Not only then has the tied house sstem a general effect in prom.ting the consumption of intoxicat- ing liquor by the inevitable improvement in the means of distribution. hut the relation between
brewer and tenant eff )rd s opportunity of putrinz

czreat pressure upon the tenants, and may thus be very injurious to the public interests' It tends moreover to hamper the action of the lieensing authority, and, often unconscioußly, to affect the activity of the police. Many owners of tied house do not of course put pressure on their tenants', but there are brewers and brewers, and a brewery corn-
winy is likely to be as anxious for dividends and as
_ ,gsreless of the methods smployed, aq other corpora- tions wit%out a conscience. Clearly the system needs to be strlnwly held in check.

div.head: BENIRDIES PROPOSND
div.p: BENIRDIES PROPOSND

Same people propose to abolish the tie altogether. but it does not seem easy to abolish what is a natural commercial development, and which is chiefly dangerous on account of the fact that the retail trade in liquor is a monopoly. The abolition oF the tie would probably be as disastrous as pro- hibitio, to many breweries, for the better-class brewers would then have the opportunity of driving their comp4itors from the field. Such a step may, however, be dismissed from consideration on the vound that it. is impossible and would merely lead to innumerable invasions. Others recommend free licensing, but past experience has shown that the remedy is worse than the disease. Owing to the bad administration of the licensing justices in Ireland, free licensing practically prevails every- where except in a few places: the tied houss system probably for this reason is very largely absent, except in Cork, and to a cersain extent in Dublin and Belfast, where licenses are beginning to be limited in number: the evils resulting from the terrible excess of licenses in most parts of the coun- try are so great as quite to overbalance the abmnce of tied houses.

The only real remedy is a stronglicensing author- ity, which will inquire into the conditions of the tenancy, and take care that the license is not granted unless the license holder is released from un'lue pressure. Nearly everywhere the licensing authority has conspicuously neglected this duty; especially remarkable, as we have seen, is their laxity in granting transfers. It is very important that on a transfer being applied for, the transferor, as well as transferee, should appear when possible, and give his reasons for leaving the house. These reasonewill often shed a ihoeof light on the ques- tion whether the house should continue to be licensed or not A justice in tne Sharnbrook divi- sion of Bedfordshire, by insisting on this rule. diminished the number of transfers by 60 per cent. Restrictions on the ease of transfer will make the brewer a great deal more careful in his choice of a tenant, and the examination of all the agreements between brewer and tenant end the voiding of any that are not so disclosed before the licensing authority will safeguard the license holder from that pressure from within, which is as dangerous to the public interest as undue pressure of competition from without. Meantime there are one or two advantages in the concentration of the ownership of public house which should be overlooked. It enables the I:cen-5 sing authority to bring pressure to bear more easily, if they wish some reform to be carried out. It also bears on the compensation question. Soppose two public housis at A, each belonging to a diff-rent firm of brewere,and two at B,belonging respectively to the same brewers all being houses of the same class in an over-licensed district. If at A a house belong- ing to one brewer is suppressed and at B. the house belonging to the -ther,each brewer is compensated at one place, for the lose sustained at the other, by a certain amount of increased trade in the remaining house. Indeed i 7 th.lcqsor tra Is conterrion that a diminution in the number of houses does not pro- duce a diminution in consumption be accepted, the brewers do not lose but actually gain, for the two houses must be more expen-ive than one to keep up. Such arrangements, however, should always be entered into with caution, and after a careful con- sideration of all the circnmstances, and that de- mands a Rood and active licensing authority, a sub- ject which we shall have presently to consider.

the geoi play of Feathers, Dobson, Morley, and Cooper. Hull v. Huddersfield. Hull made great efforts during the opening half of this match,upon their own ground, and led at half-time by a goal and two tries to nil. The visitors afterwards played up better ; still, they had ta admit defeat by fourteen points to five. Leeds v. Hunslet. Up to half-time, at Leeds. the home side had the best of this :zame. Bentley and Varlev scored a goal each, and Coleman a try, and this eventually gave Leeds the victory by seven points to two tries (six points). Leeds Parish Church v. Hull Kingston Rovers. Play was much of the "give and take "character, at Leeds, and a drawn game ot two points each was the re- sult. Corcoran scored a goal for the Churchmen, and Starks one for the Rovers. Bramley v. Castleford. A keenly-fought game by lithese teams was witnessed at Bramley. The home fifteen were credited with a dropped goal in the first half, and Castleford equalised in the second—a drawn game resulting. Manningham v. Wakefield Trinity. A victory for the home side by two tries to a goal and a try was the outcome of this game at Manningham. Walton, Gill, Crissland,and Gillings scored for their re- spective sides. Liversedge v. Batley. Stubborn play characterised the game all through this encounter at Liversedge, but ithe defence on both sides prevailed,and a pointless draw ensued. Brighouse Rangers v. Holbeck. The Rangers,playing at home,led at half-time by nine points,and eventually won by thirteen to three, South West Lancashire Cup. Swinton v. Runcorn, tat the Swinton enclosure on Wednesday, the match being a postponed fixture in connection with the tourna- ment for possession of the S3uth-West Border Cup, the opening kick was put in before a poor attendance of spectators. Runcorn showed to advantage at the out- set, and Chorley cenceded a touchdown. The home for- wards were next to the fore, and Swinton pressed until Houghton effected a fine clearance. Jolley fielded the leather in fine style, and Chorley being at fault, Swinton had an anxious time. Another minor was conceded and the kick out, supplemented by a penalty took play to the Runcorn half, where a very lengthy but very dull di,- play of the kicking abilities of the players was exhibited. Scrimmaging in neutral territory was next the order and the Runcorn halves opened out, but the result was another suecession of aimless kicks by players on either side. Play was confined to the " Lions" quarters for considerable period, and the proceedings generally were anything but inspiring, the game being of the continual " kick and rush "order. Subsequent pro- ceedings prior to the interval were in favour of the home rot, but at half time neither side had scored. The second half opened out to Swinton's advan- tage, and a strong rush by the home front rank coupled with good work by Davies, made the pro- ceedings anything but pleasing to the Runcorn par- tisans. Davies ehortly afterwards just failed to hold (he leather when a try was at his mercy. Swinton were now pressing hatly,but the stout defence of the Cheshire men frustrated the desires of the home lot. Houghton, in particular, played a fine defensive game, and the tackling of the Runcorn men was keen and vigorous. Runcorn made a rush for the home line, and after some deliberation the referee awarded a try to Messenger, and Farmer improved the occasion by landing the addition al two points. Swinton next pressed, and a score was effected at the corner, no goat resulting. R Valentine then scored a sensational try, but the goal kick was a failure. Swinton, six points; Runcorn, five points.

Follow- ing an ineffectual attempt to capture the Black- burn goal, the visitors' right again got going and meet- ing Blackshaw's centre Morgan put the teams on an equality with a shot which Chew failed to reach, the SUCCeS3 being received without a single cheer. From a corner splendidly placed by Bartley, Leach headed the ball against the crossbar. At this period Esrlestown were bringing great pressure to bear upon the visitors goal, three abortive corners being forc,cl in quick suc- cession.
